Title: Hartington - 5 Dales and 500m
Summary:
This circular walk starts and finishes in the pretty Peak District village of
Hartington
. The route follows the sparkling River Dove through some of the area's finest limestone dales, including the beautiful Beresford Dale, Wolfscote Dale and Biggin Dale. Along the way, we discover picturesque riverside paths, dramatic limestone scenery and charming villages, before returning to Hartington along quiet country tracks, with far-reaching views across the surrounding hills.
Distance:
20.9 km (13 miles)
Total Ascent:
512 metres (1,680 ft)
Leaving Hartington, we head out across open fields, enjoying wonderful panoramic views of the surrounding Derbyshire countryside. Following a well-signposted footpath, we eventually reach a gate in a stone wall before descending into Morson Wood and the beautiful Beresford Dale.
Beresford Dale is renowned for its crystal-clear waters, where the River Dove meanders gently through a wooded valley, flowing over a succession of tiny weirs. Crossing a pretty footbridge, we enter the area known as Pike Pool. Look out for the distinctive limestone column rising dramatically from the water just beyond the bridge.
Crossing the river once more, we continue with the River Dove now on our right as we enter Wolfscote Dale. This spectacular stretch of the valley is characterised by jagged limestone outcrops and impressive scenery. The dale is also rich in wildlife, with herons and Daubenton's bats among its natural inhabitants. Towering above the valley are the imposing slopes of Gratton Hill and Wolfscote Hill.
We soon arrive at the charming riverside village of Milldale, named after the two mills that once operated in the valley. From here, our route continues south before turning west, where we begin the ascent through Hall Dale, heading towards the hamlet of Stanshope.
From Stanshope, we cross open fields towards the village of Alstonefield, home to a magnificent Grade I listed 12th-century church. Leaving the village, we continue across more fields before making a steep descent into the Dove Valley, where we cross the river once again.
Heading north for a short distance, we retrace part of our morning route before turning north-east to enter Biggin Dale, our final dale of the day. A steady climb takes us to the highest point of the walk at 316 metres, rewarding us with further wonderful views across the surrounding countryside. From here, we turn west and make our way back to Hartington, completing a varied and rewarding circular walk through some of the Peak District's most beautiful dales and landscapes.
A wonderful day of riverside walking, limestone scenery, picturesque villages and spectacular views across the Derbyshire countryside.
Dogs
- Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk, be aware there may be livestock en-route.

Title: Bradshaw Valley & the Three Resevoirs Late Autumn Walk
Summary:
Join us for a brilliant moderate circular walk through the scenic Bradshaw Valley on the southern edge of the West Pennine Moors. Largely tracing the Warpers Trail section of the 32-mile Witton Weavers Way, this varied loop combines tranquil waterside paths, wooded cloughs, open pastures, and rich local industrial heritage—culminating in a classic country pub stop.
What to expect on the route:
A Chain of Three Reservoirs: Fed by Bradshaw Brook as it flows down from the moors towards Bolton, our route takes in three distinct bodies of water. We’ll explore the two impressive 19th-century upper reservoirs—Turton & Entwistle and Wayoh—originally engineered to provide a reliable water supply for the valley's booming textile mills, alongside the lower Jumbles Reservoir, added in 1971 as a compensation reservoir surrounded by lush country park woodland.
Turton Tower & Victorian Heritage: Along the way, we’ll pass Turton Tower, a Grade I listed manor house and gardens with over 600 years of history, having evolved from a defensive medieval stone pele tower into a striking 19th-century Tudor-style residence. Keep an eye out for remnants of the valley's textile past along the brook and ornate Victorian stonework where the route crosses the railway.
Wildlife & Scenery: Expect sweeping views across the reservoirs and surrounding moorland, plenty of waterfowl on the water, and peaceful stretches through mature broadleaf woodland.
Entwistle & The Strawbury Duck: Tucked in the valley between the two upper reservoirs at Entwistle, we’ll pass a tiny rural hamlet and its remote request-stop station on the Manchester–Clitheroe railway line. Towards the end of our walk, we’ll make a planned stop at the renowned Strawbury Duck pub for a well-earned refreshement, and a social before completing the final short stretch back to the start.
Walk Details & Grading
Grade: Moderate (Lowland / Hill Walk)
Distance: 11.88 km (approx. 7.4 miles)
Ascent / Descent: 252 m ascent / 257 m descent
Estimated Duration: 3.5 – 4 hours (plus time for our pub stop)
Terrain: Straightforward navigation on well-established reservoir tracks, woodland paths, riverside trails, and open field paths. Mostly on the level with one steady climb and descent in and out of the valley—expect some muddy patches after rain.
Stiles: None

Title: NOTTINGHAM Indoor Climbing (Basford) – Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads at Nottingham Climbing Centre
Climbing evenings are held regularly and we tend to go to the local pub – The Lion for refreshments and a social gathering afterwards where they have a wide variety of beverages both alcoholic and non-alcoholic.
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
Nottingham Climbing Centre
Nottingham Climbing Centre is equipped with walls and routes to suit all skill levels and groups of climbers, whether you are a novice looking to try climbing for the first time, or an experienced lead climber, you’ll find an area to challenge you. With 28 Top Ropes routes available as well as 24 Lines of Lead climbing for the more advanced individuals. In addition, 6 auto-belays are available, so there is always the opportunity to climb, even if the numbers don’t match up. The available bouldering walls also provide that extra physical and mental challenge for those looking for something slightly different from rope work. Both Bouldering and Rope Climbing routes range from 4a – 8a.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
If you've never climbed before or need a refresher, the leader will sign you into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try (it can be helpful to message the leader to let them know). If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely.
Do I need to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you answer
NO
to any of the following three questions, then you will need to arrange to be supervised. If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can sign up to this event as normal:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie yourself to the end of a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
To come along, you will need to register via this event page and to climb you will need to pay an entry fee directly to the climbing centre when you arrive, please see their
website
for up-to-date prices. We ask that all members sign up through the event page to make sure the event leader has all information of the members attending.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive)
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire a harness (again, if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire shoes and harness - £6.00*
*Equipment hire charges will be waived for your first visit to the centre!
Can I just come along and boulder?
Absolutely! Most of us do roped climbing, but if you prefer bouldering, you can sign yourself in and do it, as long as you can fill in the climbing centre's form correctly, watch their
safety video
and can answer the simple safety questions at reception on your first visit. Meet the group at the start; some others might be bouldering. We will make sure we come and find you when we have our tea break!
If you have any questions or need any more information just get in touch with the event leader by clicking on their profile below, or take a look at the
My first climbing event page
for more information.

The bouldering rooms are just as interesting as its climbing routes, over 200 bouldering problems have been organised into graded circuits to provide something for everyone.

Title: The Capital Ring - Wimbledon to Richmond
Summary:
The Capital Ring is a 120km/75 mile footpath orbiting central London at a distance of up to 10 miles from Big Ben. It was a collaboration between all of London's local authorities, and was completed in 2005. The route runs through urban and suburban outer London, utilising green space as much as possible.
This
linear
walk comprises section 6 in the south-west, running 12.5km/7.8 miles from Wimbledon to Richmond-upon-Thames and passing through Wimbledon Park, Wimbledon Common & Richmond Park.
The sights
Wimbledon Park
: 67-acre urban park that was formerly part of the grounds of Wimbledon Manor House. Purchased by Wimbledon Borough Council before WWI, and now run by the London Borough of Merton.
Wimbledon Common
: Together with Putney Common, at 1,140 acres this is the largest expanse of heathland in London, and a Site of Special Scientific Interest due to the rare flora in the area. Protected from development by its own Act of Parliament dating to 1871.
Wimbledon Windmill
: This is the last remaining hollow-post flour mill in the country. It was built in 1817, but ceased to be used as a mill in 1864. After a number of restorations, it opened as a museum in 1975.
Richmond Park
: This is the largest of the Royal Parks at 2,360 acres. It was created by Charles I as a walled deer park in 1637, but is now open to all. It is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a national nature reserve.
White Lodge
: This grade-1 listed Georgian mansion dating from 1730 is now the home of the Royal Ballet Lower School.
Pembroke Lodge
: A late 18th century mansion set on high ground in 11 acres, this was the home of Victorian prime minister Lord John Russell, and of his grandson, the philosopher and pacifist Bertrand Russell. It is now a catering, conference & wedding venue.
King Henry's Mound
: Formerly a Neolithic burial mound, this is (allegedly) where Henry VIII waited in 1536 for  a signal from the City of London that his wife Queen Anne Boleyn had been executed. There are commanding views west over the Thames Valley as far as Windsor, and St Paul's Cathedral, 12 miles to the east, can be glimpsed through a telescope installed on the Mound. This view, first created in 1710, is protected by planning restrictions.
Richmond Bridge
: This is the oldest surviving (and only Georgian) Thames bridge in London, originally constructed in 1774-7 and widened in 1937-40. It is grade-1 listed.
Richmond Palace
: Only the gate-house and couple of other small structures survive from this grand Tudor palace, built by Henry VII after 1498 to replace an earlier building destroyed by fire. It was a favourite of all the Tudors, especially Henry VIII & Elizabeth I (who died there in 1603). After the execution of Charles I in 1649, Parliament sold off the palace for building material and it was never rebuilt.
The route
(see location section for OS link):
Starting at Wimbledon Park tube station, we'll head along Home Park Road to enter & cross Wimbledon Park, leaving at the Wimbledon Park Road gate. We'll head down Wimbledon Park Road, then turn into Bathgate Road and up steep Queensmere Road to reach Wimbledon Common. We'll transit the Common via the windmill to get to the A3 at Kingston Vale. Crossing the road, we'll enter Richmond Park at the Robin Hood Gate, and climb Spankers Hill to reach the car park & refreshment kiosk near Pen Ponds, where we'll pause for lunch.
After the break, we'll carry on across Pen Ponds (with the view of White Lodge), and head down the side of Sidmouth Wood to reach Pembroke Lodge and King Henry's Mound, where we'll pause to admire the fine views.
Finally, we'll head down the hill to exit the park at Petersham Gate, and proceed to the Thames Path, which we'll follow into Richmond. The station is about half-a-mile inland from the Thames via the Palace.
Don't waste that space!
London walks are in demand, so please only book if you know you can make it. If your plans change please free up the space for someone else.
Dogs
Well-behaved dogs are welcome, but they will need to be on a lead along busy roads and footpaths and in proximity to livestock.
This particularly applies in Richmond Park, where dogs must be on a lead anywhere near deer or around lakes & ponds. If your dog is caught worrying deer or wildfowl, the Royal Parks Police could prosecute you.
Please also note that dogs are not permitted in Pembroke Lodge Gardens in Richmond Park. This unfortunately includes King Henry's Mound.
At all other times, a dog must be obedient.

Title: New Year along the New River
Summary:
Join Alex for this ten-mile winter walk taking in the New River, Hertford Heath and Broxbourne Woods.
We will meet at Broxbourne station and immediately start our route north along the New River Path. The New River is neither new nor a river: it is an artificial waterway built in the early 17th century to bring clean water to London. Following it upstream, we will skirt the edge of the towns of Broxbourne and Hoddesdon, passing the substantial houses that line the banks opposite.
After a couple of miles our route will become more industrial in character as the New River turns northwest at Rye House, running parallel to the railway. We will pass a number of pumping stations that help control the flow of water and gradually the scenery will become more picturesque as we approach the village of Stanstead St Margarets.
The path will then lead us to the pretty village of Great Amwell, where the New River widens into a pool shaded by willows. Here we will pass the church of St John the Baptist, dating from the 11th century and which preserves the village stocks in the churchyard. Leaving Great Amwell we will turn south and uphill into more open countryside before reaching Hertford Heath, where we will stop for lunch.
From here we will continue south following Ermine Street, the Roman road linking London with Lincoln and York. Our route will lead us into Broxbourne Woods nature reserve before turning east and heading gradually downhill back into the town. We will pass the 15th-century church of St Augustine before once again joining the New River briefly back to the station.

Title: Marty Memorial Walk: Stoodley Pike & Heptonstall
Summary:
This special memorial walk is an opportunity for OutdoorLads members to come together to remember Marty, celebrate the friendships and adventures we shared with him, and enjoy some of the landscapes he would have appreciated. Sadly, Marty passed away earlier this year, and we recognise that some members may only be hearing this news for the first time.
Jacob, who inspired the creation of this walk, will be sharing some of Marty's favourite poems with us during the day.
Martin Watkins joined OutdoorLads in 2011 and quickly threw himself into everything the group had to offer, attending hundreds of events over the years. In his own words, he described joining OutdoorLads as "the best thing I ever did! The adventures, the mates, the craic!! All beyond my wildest expectations!"
Many members will also remember Marty as the unsung hero of our storage unit. As our volunteer "quartermaster" for many years, he worked tirelessly to keep equipment organised and ready for the next big event. Whether behind the scenes or enjoying adventures with friends, Marty made a lasting contribution to OutdoorLads and will be fondly remembered by all who knew him.
Starting from
Hebden Bridge
, we'll head out into the dramatic South Pennine countryside for our
13.5K walk
following a route that climbs steadily onto the hills above the Calder Valley. Our journey takes us to the iconic
Stoodley Pike Monument
, one of Yorkshire's most recognisable landmarks, and a Marty favourite. We'll be rewarded with expansive views across the surrounding moors and valleys. It is usually pretty windy up here so ensure you wrap up warm and bring gloves and a hat.
From there, we'll make our way down to the canal and walk along towards Hebden Bridge, but take a climb up towards the historic village of
Heptonstall
. At
St Thomas the Apostle Church
, we'll pause for a short reading and a moment of remembrance for Marty. This will provide an opportunity for those who wish to reflect, share a quiet thought, and remember the contribution Marty made to our community and the friendships he helped create.
Continuing on, we'll follow the cobbled road and paths down to Hebden Bridge. We'll finish back in
Hebden Bridge
, where those who wish can join us afterwards to raise a glass to Marty, celebrate a life well lived, and enjoy each other's company in the way he would undoubtedly have appreciated.

Title: Dudley Wren's Nest
Summary:
8 miles, 200m ascent. Attractive woodlands, a fascinating site of geology and a look at historic parts of Dudley.
Starting from the railway station, we pass a short section of canal and see opposite a statue to William Perry, 'The Tipton Slasher', heavyweight boxing champion of Britain in the 1850s. We then enter the wilds of Dudley Woods which give us a taste of things to come.
The woods contain several humps and bumps which get more interesting as we go along. The unusual shapes were causes by limestone being washed and eroded away. The woodlands hide secret cave entrances, including a newly rediscovered secret tunnel leading half a mile up to Dudley Castle. The castle is now used as a zoo so don't be surprised if you hear unusual animal noises as we walk nearby!
We then follow a track gently uphill and through a kind of a slit between two rises on each side. This shape resembles the shape of the nest a small bird known as the Wren makes, hence its name. The path is stepped and a little steep in places; the woodlands lush and exciting. We join a main track round to the find several sites of geological interest.
White limestone edges are exposed where many different types of fossils have been found - more than 800! In fact, fossils are still being discovered, some unique to Wren's Nest. Limestone was deposited here under shallow, warm topical seas, around 315 million years ago. The fossils contain corals and other creatures from that time. We will investigate the geology trail, part of our route, and take in the views across to Dudley Castle and the Birmingham skyline in the distance.
The route then takes us through St James Priory park, passing the medieval prior ruins. We enter Coronation Gardens and see the Apollo Fountain. This is a statue of naked Greek God Apollo, with smaller figures of some of his many male lovers underneath. The centre of Dudley contains an open market which has been trading here for 800 years, around as old as the medieval castle. We walk by the castle walls, zoo entrance and back through Victoria Park Tipton to reach our starting point.

Title: Midweek Peaks: The Roaches from Danebridge on a WEDNESDAY
Summary:
Midweek Peaks is a new series of walks designed to fit flexible lifestyles and give you the opportunity to see some of the best of the Peak District when it is less busy! This walk, on a Wednesday, is a 7 mile walk from Danebridge through the woods and famous rock formation Lud's Church to the top of the Roaches, returning along the ridge.
Meeting on the bridge over the River Dane, this is the border between Cheshire and Staffordshire. You park in Cheshire and the walk is in Staffordshire. The bridge is actually a grade II listed structure of historic beauty. Our route takes us along the Dane Valley way and into Forest Wood, then up to Lud's Church.
Lud's church is an 18m chasm, caused when a landslip moved the gritstone during interglacial periods thousands of years ago. Since then, myths and legends have grown up, and this is reputed to be the site of the 'green chapel' in the medieval poem: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
Our route takes us further through woodland and up onto the dramatic peak of the Roaches. We then turn and follow the ridge back west. On the Roaches, you might see Peregrine Falcons, the small bird of prey which nests here and can reach speeds up to 124mph when diving. Red grouse are also common.
The dramatic rock formations of the Roaches are mostly gritstone, formed a little over 300 million years ago in the Carboniferous geological period. Look closely and you can see bits of grit within the rocks. These have been folded and compacted by huge geological forces over millions of years.
On a clear day, you can see all the way to Winter Hill in the North, Wales to the West and the Shropshire Hills to the South West. Our descent passes below Hangingstone - an outcrop which seems to hang off the main Roaches ridge forming a dramatic western end.
Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk. Our planned route is

. We will return to Danebridge in good time to beat the traffic on your return home. If you have time, the Wincle Brewery Tearoom is open until 4.30pm, so why not check it out before heading home.

Title: Kenilworth Castle Loops
Summary:
Join Elliott on his assessment walk in Kenilworth!
A circular walk from Kenilworth station of 7.9 miles (12.8 km) mostly flat with approximately 82m of ascent. There are some great views of Kenilworth Castle from walking on footpaths around it and this walk aims to cover most of these viewpoints.
Kenilworth Castle was established in 1120, and endured one of the longest sieges in medieval English history. The height of the castle was during the reign of Elizabeth where, Robert Dudley spent a fortune turning it into a showpiece to impress the Queen. The castle was slighted in 1650 during the English Civil War, with some of the walls pulled down and the moat drained.
The route
We will depart from Kenilworth Station heading Southwest out of the town, aiming for Rounds Hill road, and heading south across some fields till we join the Centenary Way heading north towards the Castle. The Lunch Stop will be outside Kenilworth Castle, probably partly round the moat walk. After lunch we will finish the moat walk, and then do the Pleasance Circular. We might spot some Alpaca's in the farm on our right before passing by the earthworks of King Henry V’s moated pleasure garden, but mostly just getting far enough away from the castle to see some really good views of it. Once back at the Castle (for the final time) we will pass through Abbey Fields Park, (named after the ruined Abbey in its centre) and along the side of the Abbey’s old carp ponds. Before a short stretch through Kenilworth before returning to the station.

Title: Chalkie Walkie
Summary:
Always a popular starting point this winter hike takes us from Petersfield town in a big circle through lovely countryside. On route there are various points of interest and history.
Click on this
Link
to view the route (opens OS Maps)
A Few Features:
Petersfield
Located just 15 miles north of Portsmouth this historic market town can trace its roots right the way back to Norman times. Back then it would have been classed as a 'New Town'. The town church dates to 1120 and still boasts many of its original features. The main square proudly features an equestrian statue of King William III.
Shipwrights Way
We'll make use of this track several times during our hike. Its origins go right the way back to Tudor times and would have been the route to take timber to the coast for building warships. Some 50 miles long it starts in Alice Holt Forest near Farnham and goes all the way to Portsmouth Dockyard.
Queen Elizabeth Country Park
At just over 2000 acres this vast area offers a real escape from the hustle and bustle of life. Part of our hike will take in the park and it is easy to forget the busy A3 isn't too far away. The park was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1976 and came about by the merging of two separate green spaces. There is clearly a good food source here as on my recce walk I witnessed flocks of literally hundreds of pigeons!
Buriton Chalk Pit
Now a 14 acre Local Nature Reserve this site was once a bustling working pit removing vast quantities of chalk from the land. It was only after World War II that operations ceased. In its heyday chalk would have been removed on an industrial scale and burnt in onsite lime kilns. The resulting lime would have then been used as a building material.
Buriton Village
The village started life as a Saxon settlement and is listed in the Domesday Book. At the time there were probably less than 100 residents. Farming would have been the main source of work and people would have lived in simple wooden huts with thatched roofs.
St Mary's Church in the centre of the village is believed to have been built in the late 12th century. It's tower being rebuilt in 1714 after the original burned down. Surprisingly, until the late 1800s the village church was the 'mother' church of the area, and Petersfield church being the 'daughter'.
In the 18th century the construction of a main road from London to Portsmouth brought many people to the village. The two big pubs would have probably been a hive of activity with frequent stagecoach arrivals.

Title: Stretford to Manchester -GM20
Summary:
This is stage 20 of 20 on the Greater Manchester Ringway, a 200 mile (322km) walking trail exploring all 10 boroughs of Greater Manchester. You can find out more about it

.
The final stage of the GM Ringway connects Stretford with Manchester city centre via a series of largely traffic-free waterside paths. The route includes some little-known green spaces and an astonishing series of museums and heritage sites from every age, making it a worthwhile full-day outing.
Highlights include:
The striking structure of Imperial War Museum North, designed by US architect Daniel Libeskind
The vibrant waterside attractions of Salford Quays
The Grade I-listed Ordsall Hall, a 15th-century manor house surrounded by Elizabethan gardens
Riverside paths along the Manchester Ship Canal and River Irwell, the surprisingly peaceful waterways separating the cities of Manchester and Salford
A wander between green and traffic-free spaces of the city centre.
Note that parts of the trail may be damp, muddy and slippery at any time of year and especially after periods of wet weather.

Title: Weald and Downland: Trek the Hills with Brows so Jolly!
Summary:
As the afternoon of this event comprises a visit to the Weald and Downland Living Museum, the cost to all members is £16.50.
During Advent, the Weald and Downland open-air museum near Chichester explores how people prepared for Christmas in earlier centuries. In the historic buildings there one finds re-enactors in period dress (and a green Father Christmas) demonstrating crafts, food preparation and winter housekeeping. Advent was traditionally a period of preparation and fasting, with the Christmas decoration and feasting beginning on Christmas Day, so the the houses won't be turned into festive grottoes, but this event will still overflow with festivity and fellowship. We'll walk deep and high into the South Downs National Park at its loveliest, but we'll return by bus to the starting point.
My thanks go to the lovely Josh Zarn for suggesting this event.
The sights:
Chichester:
A cathedral city of Roman origin (Noviomagus Reginorum) founded soon afer the Claudian invasion of 43 AD. Many Georgian buildings and a thriving arts scene. The chief sights are:
City walls:
Originally Roman, c 200 AD, four metres wide and five metres high in places. 80 per cent complete, making them the most intact circuit of Roman town defences in Southern England;
Pallant House Gallery:
The original Pallant House was built 1712-13 is one of Chichester's finest Georgian houses. It is rather upstaged by the admittedly very fine Gallery of 2003-6 by Colin St John Wilson, architect of the British Library. The third design for this was eventually accepted after the first two were reviled;
South and North Pallant:
Attractive historic streets of C18 and early C19 town houses, predominantly in brick or stucco, with sash windows, classical doorcases, cornices and tiled roofs. Their varied façades and rooflines preserve the character of Georgian Chichester;
St Martin’s Street and St Martin’s Square:
A compact historic area containing C18 town houses with classical detailing, including rusticated ground floors, pilasters, cornices and pedimented doorways. No. 8 St Martin’s Square is particularly distinguished for its red-brick façade and central entrance.
East Lavant:
Beside the river with a lovely intricate yet relaxed plan. Brick, flint and thatched cottages and a superb view north to the Downs. St Mary's Church is C12 and C13 with a plain brick tower of 1671 and all the rest a Victorian restoration of 1863.
St Roche's Hill and the Trundle:
206 m in elevation. The Trundle (Old English 'Tryndel' or 'circle') is an Iron Age hill fort built around a Neolithic causewayed enclosure. Subsequent history involves a chapel to St Roche (lost), a Civil War encampment and a viewing area to Goodwood Racecourse. There are wonderful views to be had, north over the Weald and south over the Sussex Plain and the Sea.
Goodwood:
We won't see the late C18 stately home and we'll only see the aerodrome, car racing circuit and site of the Goodwood Revival at a distance, but we'll get a grandstand view of the grandstands of the famous racecourse. 'Glorious Goodwood' earned its honorific by being 180m up, and set in sublime countryside. It was laid out in 1801 as a private military racecourse. The current stands are the March Stand of 1980, the Charlton Stand of 1989 and the Sussex Stand of 1990, the latter by Arup Associates.
Singleton:
A small village in the Lavant Valley below the South Downs escarpment. Historic core of flint and brick cottages, tile-hung elevations and tiled roofs. St Mary’s Church retains an early C11 tower, with C13 nave and aisle arcades and C15 alterations. The surrounding downland and farmland offer a timeless rural setting.
Weald and Downland Living Museum, Singleton:
Open-air museum founded in 1970, occupying a 40-acre site on the South Downs. More than 50 historic buildings, dismantled at their original sites and re-erected here, illustrate vernacular architecture and rural life over a millennium. Includes medieval timber-framed houses, C17–C19 cottages, barns, workshops and a working watermill. Traditional materials and techniques include timber framing, wattle and daub, thatch, clay tiles and local stone. Especially valuable for presenting historic buildings within their original functional contexts.
The
route
(click the link to see the walk at the OS website)
:
Leaving the station we will cross the town centre along South and North Pallant, then through St Martin's Street and St Martin's Square to Priory Lane. At the top of New Park Road we'll cross Spitalfield Lane to walk north along College Lane out to Summersdale suburb. Beyond that, the West Sussex Literary Trail running along Fordwater Road will take us out of the town into the countryside to East Lavant to begin ascending the Downs by way of Chalk Pit Lane. At the top of the lane, we'll cross the Trundle, follow Knight's Hill towards Charlton before a footpath veers off towards Singleton. Walking west along Charlton Road and south along Town Road will bring us to the museum.
Getting the bus back
The Stagecoach no. 60 bus runs from outside the museum in Singleton to Chichester at 10 and 40 minutes past and costs £3.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them, although there will be lots of road walking in town and may be some fields with livestock. Dogs are encouraged at the museum, but because of free-range lifestock there, they will have to be on a short lead of at most 1.2 m, and extendable or flexi-leads are not permitted. Dogs are also not permitted in a few buildings. A dog off the lead must be obedient.

Nottingham Climbing Centre

Title: Nottingham Bouldering (Lenton) - MONDAY - Beginners Welcome
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Nottingham’s newest bouldering venue

Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?

As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.

Title: Leeds LGBTQ+ Social Climbing Night
Summary:
Leeds LGBTQ+ Social Climbing Night!
Join us for the Leeds LBGTQ+ social climbing night, starting with a climb followed by a pint at Queens Court! This is an informal event with the cost being the standard entry fee to the centre.
So.... a bit about climbing and the centre….
Climbing is a total body workout. It is not just about strength, but requires balance, problem solving and planning. Climbing routes are like puzzles that might need some breaking down, planning or practice. Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends and develop your climbing skills.
The Big Depot is our venue. Prior to being redeveloped by the company, it was (and to many still is) known as The Leeds Wall. It was built from the University of Leeds in 1964 and is widely regarded as the world’s first permanent indoor climbing wall.
Today it provides an enormous variety of angles and styles of climbs. With grades for all abilities any climber will enjoy the routes here. It is also a great place to start climbing, so if you want to take the step into the world of climbing this is the place to try it.
To come along, please book on to this event and also register with The Big Depot if you have not done so before (
https://www.depotclimbing.co.uk/big-depot/registrations/
) Please choose the '18+ Unsupervised Climbers' form – and pay particular attention to the questions as they are almost designed to trip you up!
You can pay at the centre on arrival or online beforehand.
I’m new to climbing – can I come along?
Yes! New climbers are very welcome! Just let us know by messaging the event leader or co-leader, so we can arrange for you to be signed into the climbing centre as a supervised climber so that you can come and give it a try.
If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we’d recommend that you attend a formal beginner climbing course at the centre or separately.
Please note that we are limited by the climbing centre as to the number of novice climbers we can supervise, according to the number of experienced people / staff available at the event.
Do I have to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can climb without supervision:
• Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
• Can you tie in to a rope using the correct knots?
• Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
If all that is meaningless to you – you’ll need to be supervised and then attend a course if you want to climb unsupervised.
What other Climbing events do OutdoorLads Run?
We run regular indoor climbing and bouldering events across the UK. We are always keen to put more on, so if you fancy climbing in your local area contact a climbing leader and we can see what we can arrange.

While Fabian runs an outdoor guiding and instructing company and is a qualified Rock Climbing Instructor, he attends these events for the social side. He is not here to do the day job!

Title: England's Transport Spine: Gayton, Bugbrooke & Pattishall
Summary:
Here's the first in a series of rural walks especially planned for the winter months which is - hopefully - firm under foot, whatever the weather has thrown at us recently!
This part of
West Northamptonshire
offers a fascinating insight into how transport links have evolved along the spine of England through the centuries;
The A5 -
Watling Street
- was built by the Romans. Starting as London's
Edgware Road
from Marble Arch, it passes through Towcester on its way to Hinckley in Leicestershire
In 1796, the
Grand Union Canal
opened here - enabling the carriage of heavy freight traffic - albeit rather slowly!
Then, in 1838, the
London & Birmingham Railway
opened for traffic through Northamptonshire, revolutionising journey times for freight and passengers
The final step-change came in 1959 with the opening of the Northamptonshire stretch of the
M1 Motorway
, bringing much needed relief to the towns and villages along the old A5
Despite all of these transport corridors being visible during our walk, this is actually a very rural and peaceful part of the rolling landscape of West Northamptonshire.
Starting under the splendid millennium village sign in
Gayton
, we'll head across the fields and swoop down to cross what is now known as the West Coast Mainline before joining the towpath of the Grand Union Canal. With something in excess of 350 trains passing along this stretch of line within a 24-hour period on a typical Saturday, it's not difficult to understand the original argument to expand capacity and give this Victorian route some relief by building HS2...
We'll follow the towpath for a couple of miles to the village of
Bugbrooke
where we'll pause for a picnic lunch in the churchyard. Immediately opposite, the
Five Bells
offers an opportunity for a drink as well!
After lunch we return briefly to the canal before heading up across the fields to the village of
Pattishall
. Before the M1 was built, the village offered petrol stations and accommodation on this busy stretch of the A5. But Pattishall occupies a particularly interesting position because it's also on
Banbury Lane
- one of the oldest surviving routeways in central England. It was used from the medieval period through the 18th and 19th centuries to move cattle and sheep.
A couple of fields take us to the charming village of
Eastcote
before our final leg brings us back to our starting point in Gayton.

Our walk includes a canal towpath, some short stretches on country roads and village streets. We may encounter sheep, lambs, cows or horses and there are a few fields where landowner signs request dogs on a lead.

Title: Culbin Forest, the Gut and the Viewing Tower
Summary:
As we fast approach the shortest day of the year, join your OutdoorLads friends for a walk in the Forest.
This is a 9km circular walk, with under 100m of ascent and decent throughout. The bulk of the route is in forest with about 1.5km along the shore by the mudflats of Findhorn Bay.
Culbin Forest used to be an area of shifting sand dunes which had been damaged by storms over the centuries, burying villages in the process. The Forestry Commission bought the land in the 1920s and planted Corsican and Scots Pine to stabilise the dunes and to provide timber. Other trees have also moved in. The forest is dotted with cultural and historical interest, explained on interpretation boards en route. One f the highlights is the viewing tower erected at the highest point in the forest offering views (weather permitting) in all directions.
The stretch along the shore could give good views of bird life that winters here, escaping harsher conditions further north.
The terrain is mostly trail paths. One section has gorse closing in on both sides so expect a prick or two on your lower legs! There's a steep but short ascent up to the base of the viewing tower.

Title: The Falls of Foyers and Loch Ness shoreline
Summary:
This is a two hour walk, just under three miles, from the loch-side village of Foyers on the eastern shore of Loch Ness.
The real highlight are the Falls of Foyers that plunge down a gorge, with the waters on their way to Loch Ness. It's a truly impressive sight and we get to see the Falls from two purpose-built viewing points - great spots for photos. The more rain we've had, the better the falls. NB If then hydro plant is taking water higher up for power generation, the falls will be reduced in power, but we'll be very unlucky for this to happen.
The walk continues down through beautiful mixed woodland eventually arriving at the side of Loch Ness. We follow the shore a short way before beginning our ascent, but not before we pass some intriguing huts by the loch and a memorial.
There is a cafe at the start / finish so hopefully it will be open and we can have a brew / cake before all heading home.

Title: Wednesday Wander: A Happy Valley at Christmas
Summary:
Enjoy a pre-Christmas hike around the popular Happy Valley area of Coulsdon. The terrain will be varied and we'll see some stunning scenery on route. If that wasn't enough there are plenty of historic points and landmarks to keep us entertained. Near the end we can also enjoy a Christmas drink before our return.
Click on this
Link
to view the route (opens OS Maps)
A Few Features:
Farthing Downs
The most extensive area of semi-natural downland left in London.  Views are offered over a great distance.  There are also cows roaming freely as they graze.  History is also paramount here.  The site is believed to go back to Neolithic times with evidence of a historical past dotted around.
St Peter and St Paul Church
Work started on the church before 1086 and it is still in use today.  The church is famous for having a wall painting believed to have been done around 1170.  Amazingly, the painting was only discovered during restoration works in 1870-1.  It has been described as “perhaps the most interesting ancient wall-painting in England”.
Happy Valley
The general name for the whole area.  Originally, things were known as the Coulsdon Greenbelt Lands.  That is obviously quite a stuffy name so in 1970 the name was changed to Happy Valley Park.
St Lawrence's Hospital Burial Ground
The Caterham Metropolitan Asylum, later known as St Lawrence’s Hospital opened in 1870. Between this time and 1915 the burial ground was used to facilitate the hospital.  The site is now a place of history but graves and a memorial garden remain.  The site of the former chapel is visible.
Coulsdon Common
Another lovely green space where fields and woodland meet.  As with other areas we pass through it is easy to forget we are in London.
Kenley Airfield
RAF Kenley was a main operating airfield from 1917 to 1959.  It saw heavy use during both World Wars.  Sadly, few buildings remain and the Control Tower itself was demolished following fire in 1978.  That said it is thought to be one of the best preserved Second World War RAF fighter stations.  Some land has been used for housing but the site is still active.  The RAF 2 Flying Training School are still an active presence. Due to this the site falls under the Ministry of Defence.

Title: SE500 Hampstead Heath
Summary:
This walk consists of 2 parts:
Part 1 - West Hampstead to Highgate Wood
- 11K (7 miles). This is our lunch stop.
Part 2 -(optional) SE500 - walk back via a different route
- total 20.8K (13 miles) and 509m ascent.
Everyone
will walk
Part 1
first, then you can choose whether to continue with
Part 2
or get the train back.
Enjoy some of the best of London with a walk through Hampstead Heath, including relaxed late autumn woodlands, crispy leafs and open parkland, ideal for chilling out before Christmas. We also pass a wealth of history, historic buildings and plaques to famous people who lived in Hampstead.
This part of London is hilly in places: the slopes, ups and downs add up to 500m of ascent if completing the whole route. This makes it one of the SE500 series of walks, designed as a bit of a challenge to burn off around 2000 calories over the day! The paths are good, with a few steps and steeper slopes in Highgate Woods to make up the ascent.
This walk marks a milestone for the SE500 walks. This will be the 16th walk. Adding up all the ascents together, including todays, the walks will total over 9000m of height gain, topping Mount Everest!
The streets of Hampstead exude opulence and history, evidenced in fine houses and plaques to historic figures who lived here. See the house on the left of Frognal street, which has a historic blue plaque to Sir Harold Gillies (1882-1960), a pioneer plastic surgeon. A little further up the same road is a blue plaque on the right to Tamara Karsavina (1885-1978), a ballerina. On the left is a plaque to Kathleen Ferrier (1912-1953), an English contralto singer. Then, a little further a plaque to Charles de Gaulle (1890-1970), the famous French leader who lived here for a while.
We pass National Trust Fenton House, with it’s fine frontage gates. This was a 17th century merchants house. Then, our first brush with the wilds of the upper part of Hampstead Heath woodlands, and a descent through West Heath woodlands to the landscaped Golder’s Hill parkland. Heading uphill, we find The Hill Garden and Pergola, where you may pop through the archway to see the formal gardens (no dogs beyond the arch). This was the dream of Lord Leverhulme, a wealthy idealist and patron of the arts.
Our wander through beautiful woodlands continues and enters the formal grounds of Kenwood House. The house dates from the 17th century, contains notable art work and has a fine viewpoint across London. We’ll see the view and peek at the walled garden, before traversing more of the Heath. Then, a climb through exclusive residential backwaters to Highgate.
Following the roads for a bit, we pass the house of A.E. Housman, poet and author of A Shropshire Lad. He wrote beautiful love poetry to his male lover, Moses Jackson, and made coded criticisms of the law at a time when homosexuality was banned.
We then enter Highgate Wood, where there is a small café stall and a place for us to rest for lunch. If you wish to complete your walk here, then turn right as we are about to enter the woods, from where it is a short 5 minutes walk to Highgate Tube station.
(Trains back from Highgate tube, Northern Line southbound, changing at Kentish Town for Thameslink -1 stop to West Hampstead Thameslink).
Continuing after lunch, there are quite a few ups and downs and stepped paths through the woods which will tot up more of our ascent. After some quiet back streets, we enter Waterlow Park and pass the Jewish Cemetery where Michael Faraday's grave is marked, the famous Victorian scientist. Then, it's downhill to Hampstead men's pond.
After the pond, we again gain excellent views of London from Parliament Hill, and wander across the edge of the Heath to return to West Hampstead through opulent residential streets, crossing a few roads along the way. Follow the
route
on OS Maps. Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk.

Title: Indoor Climbing MANCHESTER - Beginners welcome!
Summary:
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Join us for an evening of climbing in one of the UK's top climbing centres. Whether you are new to climbing or a seasoned climber, this centre offers something for everyone with a huge selection of routes including top rope, lead and auto belay.
Prefer to boulder? That's well catered for as well, with an extensive modern bouldering area ensuring there is plenty to keep you busy, or you can swap between climbing and bouldering on the same night.
Climbing is the main focus of the event, but this is also a great chance to meet other members and build lasting friendships. Many Outdoor Lads members join through climbing, so if you're new to the group and want to know more, come along and chat over a cuppa during the tea and cake break.
What to expect on your first climb with us?
If you are an experienced climber and have passed the centre's proficiency test, we'll pair you up with a climbing buddy and you'll be out exploring the centre in no time.
If you have never climbed before or think you could do with a refresher, we offer supervised climbing sessions with one of our leaders, subject to availability. That session will focus on introducing you to climbing, making sure you get plenty of time on the wall whilst also showing you how to belay safely. Due to the centre's rules, we are limited in the number of climbers the leader is able to supervise in each session so if you think you may need a supervised session,
please contact the leader before signing up to make sure there is enough space.
As a general guide, if you answer "no" to any of the following questions, you should opt for a supervised session:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie into a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay and lower down another climber correctly and confidently?
After a few supervised sessions, you should be ready to complete the centre's proficiency test and once that has been passed, you'll be able to climb with the rest of the group.
Everything else you need to know
You will need to register with Big Depot before your first visit to the centre but you only need to do this once. If you are an experienced climber, you can save time and do this online
here
, selecting the 18+ unsupervised option. This also applies if you just want to boulder, just select the relevant options during the registration. If you are a beginner and require a supervised session, the leader will help register you when you are at the centre.
Photos provided by Sieh and Dexmonster.
Difficulty & Distance: There is a range of routes of varying difficulty, but there should be something to suit everybody

Bouldering is a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems', as they are referred to, tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Title: Sheffield LGBTQ+ Climbing night - beginners welcome!
Summary:
Join us for the Sheffield LBGTQ+ climbing night, starting with a social meet-up followed by some climbing. This will be an informal event, with team member(s) of the climbing centre there to offer advice and some supervision. The cost is the standard entry fee to the centre. Informal tuition will also be able from OutdoorLads, but this is dependent on numbers.
Anyone can join the event, but please do sign up here so we can pass numbers on to the climbing centre.
So.... a bit about climbing and the centre..
Climbing is a total body workout. It is not just about strength, but requires balance, problem solving and planning. Climbing routes are like puzzles that might need some breaking down, planning or practice. Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends and develop your climbing skills.
Awesome Walls Sheffield was the first climbing centre to be awarded ‘National Performance Centre’ status by the British Mountaineering Council. They provide the biggest climbing walls encompassing the widest variety of angles and styles of climbs. With grades for all abilities any climber will enjoy the routes here. It is also a great place to start climbing, so if you want to take the step into the world of climbing this is the place to try it.
To come along, please book on to this event and also register with Awesome Walls Sheffield if you have not done so before (
https://www.awesomewalls.co.uk/sheffield-registration/)
Please choose the 'mixed use' form. You can pay at the centre on arrival or online beforehand. If you pay in person at the centre a small discount is available if you mention you're with ODL.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
Yes! Beginners are very welcome. If you've never climbed before, just let us know by messaging the event leader or co-leader, so we can arrange for you to be signed into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try. If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely. Please note that we are limited by the climbing centre as to the number of novice climbers we can supervise, according to the number of experienced people / staff available at the event.
Do I have to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can climb without supervision:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie in to a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
What other Climbing events do OutdoorLads Run?
We run regular indoor climbing and bouldering events across the UK. We are always keen to put more on, so if you fancy climbing in your local area contact a climbing leader and we can see what we can arrange.

Title: SCRT #1 Twixmas on the Steel Cotton Rail Trail
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a brilliant Twixmas day out along the borders of Greater Manchester!
We’ll start a brand-new adventure following a section of the Steel, Cotton and Rail Trail from Manchester to Guide Bridge.
Tracing the path of the Ashton Canal, this walk serves as a gentle and leisurely introduction to a series of walks that will eventually take us all the way from Manchester (the cotton city) to Sheffield (the steel city) via the Hope Valley—following the historic route where early 20th-century workers escaped their industrial cities for the clean air of the Peak District.
​Whether you're a regular or joining us for your very first OutdoorLads event, this walk offers a gentle way to burn off a few Christmas calories, enjoy an escape from the family dramas and festive television, and take in a great mix of industrial heritage and urban-fringe nature—a perfect day out to stretch your legs and catch up with friends!
​
What to Expect
​Ashton Canal & Waterside Stroll
: Enjoy flat, peaceful walking along the Ashton Canal towpath as we transition smoothly away from the city buzz toward Guide Bridge.
​Industrial & Railway Heritage
: Discover the rich roots of the region's manufacturing and transport history, following paths that echo the historic journeys between the cotton and steel capitals.
​Festive Escape
: Shake off the festive cobwebs, burn off a few Christmas calories, and enjoy a break from family dramas and Christmas TV in the fresh air.
Social Finish
: Wrap up the walk in Guide Bridge with the option to grab a well-deserved post-walk drink or bite to eat at a cozy local spot with the group!
​Key Details & Practicalities
​Distance & Elevation
: Approximately 5.6 miles with a gentle, manageable, and largely flat profile—the ideal starting point to get those New Year's exercise and outdoors resolutions to a flying start.
​
Terrain
: Mix of canal towpaths, urban paths, and easy trail tracks.
​Atmosphere
: Relaxed, inclusive, and social—ideal for making connections in a supportive outdoor environment. This is an ideal walk to get reacquainted with hiking.
​This is a dog friendly event - so please bring your pooches along! (Please ensure dogs are kept on a lead where appropriate).

Title: Brighton’s Weird and Wonderful Walk with Nelly and Stuart
Summary:
Join Nelly and Stuart for a fun city walk exploring Brighton’s weird and wonderful landmarks, hidden gems and famous film locations. Get some inspiration for your next movie night!
Forget the usual tourist trail! We’ll venture beyond Brighton’s best-known sights to discover some of the city’s lesser-known treasures, uncover fascinating stories and visit places you might recognise from the big screen.
This circular walk starts and finishes at Brighton Railway Station, taking us through the heart of the city before heading out for an enjoyable stroll along the seafront.
Walk distance:
5.2 miles
Route:
You can follow the route on
OS Maps
Follow the Walk Highlights
Richard's Garage
- A pair of early 1950s petrol pumps - The pumps were in operation until 2010 and are believed to be among the earliest in Brighton.
The smallest art gallery in Brighton
- Dog and Bone Art Gallery in Powis Square
The Vaults in the St Nicolas Rest Garden
- Built in 1841 by Regency architect Amon Henry Wilds, the buildings are made from stone and stucco. They have a simple semi-Gothic design, with Tudor-style arches, buttresses, pinnacles and decorative stonework.
The Church of St Nicolas
, the patron saint of sailors and fishermen. The earliest known mention of a church in Brighthelmstone, the old name for Brighton, dates back to the Domesday Book, written around 1085. -
More info
-
https://www.stnicholasbrighton.org.uk/church/history-of-the-church/
Anna's Museum
- a private collection of natural history finds displayed in the window by a local taxidermist.
Montpelier Villas
- high class mid 19th century residential district - outstanding examples of Regency and Victorian architecture.
More info
-
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montpelier,_Brighton
St Anne's Well Garden
- Home to a
chalybeate spring
a natural mineral spring that contains high levels of iron salts. The garden also has links to early film making, between 1892 and 1904, film pioneer George Albert Smith rented the gardens and built a glass studio. It was an important place in early film history, where he experimented with colour films and close-up shots that helped shape modern cinema. More info -
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Ann%27s_Well_Gardens,_Hove
Weston Pavilion
- the baby brother to the Royal Pavilion on Western Terrace -
More info
-
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Pavilion
Palmeira Square and Adelaide Crescent
- A movie location for the 2001 film '
Me Without You
' film starring Anna Friel, Michelle Williams, and Oliver Milburn, and written and directed by Sandra Goldbacher.
Brunswick Terrace
- Location for the key scenes of the 1953 comedy movie '
Genevieve'
about two couples in the London to Brighton veteran car rally.
Also,
Dirty Weekend
, a 1993 film directed by Michael Winner.
Embassy Court
- Location for 2005 British-American dark fantasy film
MirrorMask
designed and directed by Dave McKean, and written by Neil Gaiman
West Pier

Title: Adel woods and Eccup reservoir circular
Summary:
Join me for a circular approximately 8 / 8.5 miles walk taking in the beautiful surroundings of
Eccup Reservoir
and the rolling countryside on the northern edge of Leeds. With around 400 feet of ascent, this is a moderately paced walk. We'll meet at the car park at the start of the walk, following paths through open farmland and quiet lanes before reaching the reservoir, one of Yorkshire's largest bodies of water and an important haven for wildlife.
The route circles much of the reservoir, offering expansive waterside views and woodland sections. Along the way we'll pass historic farms, attractive rural landscapes and peaceful trails. It is mainly flat, and the paths are established, though it can be muddy in places, so please wear some sturdy walking boots. For some sections of the route we will walk on country roads.
A great opportunity to enjoy fresh air, good company and some of the finest green spaces right on Leeds' doorstep.
If the event is fully booked:
please
join the waiting list as people frequently drop out during the week before an event and you are likely to get a place on the walk.
If this is your first OutdoorLads walk event,
we’ll make sure you feel welcome. Please
check out the My First Event page
, and don’t hesitate to drop me a message if you have questions or want to know more about this walk.

Title: London Bouldering Saturday Morning - All Abilities welcome!
Summary:
Come and join OutdoorLads for some bouldering in central London!
If you have not been to one of the London Climbing Centres you will need to pre-register
HERE
. You only need to register once to use any of their 8 centres in London.
This event is for members of all levels of experience and all are welcome to come along to any of the sessions.
Bouldering is a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems', as they are referred to, tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes the activities excellent for newcomers to the sport.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
First time boulderer?
If you have never tried bouldering before, the event leader can give you a short introduction to get you started and give a few a few pointers on technique. After which we will join in with the rest of the group.
All those attending the event must also be aware of the centre's own terms and conditions of participation and abide by them, along with any instructions given by the centre’s staff. Everyone must also take responsibility for their own safety while participating in Indoor climbing events.
Experienced boulderer?
Simply register with the wall and turn up on the day!
As above, all attending the event must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you are at all times responsible for your own safety and so should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads volunteers or other experienced climbers.
Difficulty & Distance: With climbs at every grade from complete beginner to seasoned pro, you decide how hard it gets!

Title: NOTTINGHAM Indoor Climbing (Basford) – Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads at Nottingham Climbing Centre
Climbing evenings are held regularly and we tend to go to the local pub – The Lion for refreshments and a social gathering afterwards where they have a wide variety of beverages both alcoholic and non-alcoholic.
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
Nottingham Climbing Centre
Nottingham Climbing Centre is equipped with walls and routes to suit all skill levels and groups of climbers, whether you are a novice looking to try climbing for the first time, or an experienced lead climber, you’ll find an area to challenge you. With 28 Top Ropes routes available as well as 24 Lines of Lead climbing for the more advanced individuals. In addition, 6 auto-belays are available, so there is always the opportunity to climb, even if the numbers don’t match up. The available bouldering walls also provide that extra physical and mental challenge for those looking for something slightly different from rope work. Both Bouldering and Rope Climbing routes range from 4a – 8a.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
If you've never climbed before or need a refresher, the leader will sign you into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try (it can be helpful to message the leader to let them know). If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely.
Do I need to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you answer
NO
to any of the following three questions, then you will need to arrange to be supervised. If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can sign up to this event as normal:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie yourself to the end of a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
To come along, you will need to register via this event page and to climb you will need to pay an entry fee directly to the climbing centre when you arrive, please see their
website
for up-to-date prices. We ask that all members sign up through the event page to make sure the event leader has all information of the members attending.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive)
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire a harness (again, if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire shoes and harness - £6.00*
*Equipment hire charges will be waived for your first visit to the centre!
Can I just come along and boulder?
Absolutely! Most of us do roped climbing, but if you prefer bouldering, you can sign yourself in and do it, as long as you can fill in the climbing centre's form correctly, watch their
safety video
and can answer the simple safety questions at reception on your first visit. Meet the group at the start; some others might be bouldering. We will make sure we come and find you when we have our tea break!

Title: Outdoor First Aid Course for Leaders - Bristol
Summary:
This training course is funded by OutdoorLads for leaders, especially Mountain Walk Leaders, Outdoor/Sport Climbing Leaders, and Mountain Biking Leaders.
These leaders are required by our insurance policy to have had Outdoor First Aid training to lead these event types. Other outdoor event leaders, including lowland and hill leaders, may book on to this course, but those required to complete the training will be prioritised should a waitlist develop.
This 16-hour outdoor first aid course deals with issues involved with the long term care of casualties in a remote setting. It is often referred to as a wilderness first aid or a remote first aid.
The outdoor first aid course includes primary and secondary surveys of a casualty, we also look at first aid equipment and how you may adapt and improvise your own equipment to support your first aid kit.
A lot more emphasis is placed on incident management and relaying information to rescue teams in the outdoors. We assume minimal outdoor equipment is available and there are plenty of opportunities to practice first aid.
This 2 day (16 hour) course is recognised by the National Governing Bodies such as the Mountain Leader Training, British Canoe Union, British Cycling, British Association of Snowsport Instructors etc.
Please note:
First Aid is an active, practical, participative and interactive subject. Participants are normally expected to be physically fit and able to kneel, twist and bend over simulated casualties, to sit on the floor, perform simulated CPR, roll, help roll and help lift simulated casualties.
We hope candidates will act as simulated casualties. This will involve hands on, being touched and touching, sometimes placing hands just under outer layers of clothing if multiple layers are being worn, please raise this with the trainer if this would make you uncomfortable
For indoor sessions, please wear loose, comfortable clothing, not skirts, shorts or low cut tops. Also, please do not wear lipstick, lip gloss or lip balms as this hinders the effective cleaning of the manikins.
This course will also involve outdoor sessions; please make sure you bring clothing appropriate to the weather conditions such as warm base layers and full body waterproof cover. You will be laying on the ground and rolling around, and it's early Spring, so warm and waterproof is the way to go.
By attending a First Aid Academy event, you consent to being photographed and/or videoed. These photographs may appear in promotional material, social media and may be use to promote future First Aid Academy events.
Event cost
To help us ensure that those that book on to this event are committed to it, we're asking Leaders to pay £15. This payment will be refunded in full once attendance on the course is confirmed after the event. If you cancel before the event and we can fill your place, you will be refunded in full, but otherwise your booking on this event is subject to the
OutdoorLads refund policy
.
OutdoorLads will subsidise your course fee, you are responsible for your own travel, food and accommodation costs. The course lasts for two days, starting early each morning and finishing in the evening each day and you are required to attend both days.
Please note that places on this are for leaders, and those who have already applied to become leaders. If you have any doubts, please contact the OutdoorLads office to discuss.

Title: Cheddar Chills & Cozy Fires: Winter Weekend in the Mendips
Summary:
Join us for a fantastic winter weekend in the heart of Somerset!
Based at a comfortable, cozy base nestled right at the edge of the Mendip Hills, we’ll be exploring one of Britain’s most spectacular natural wonders. Whether you are a regular hostel-goer or this is your very first OutdoorLads event, you’re guaranteed a weekend of great walking, brilliant company, and plenty of laughs.
The Weekend Plan
Friday: Welcome & The Big Buffet
Arrive from
5:00 pm
onwards to find your bed, unpack, and settle in.
We’ll kick off the weekend with our
classic OutdoorLads shared welcome buffet
. Rather than cooking a full meal on Friday night,
we ask everyone to bring a contribution to share
—think pies, quiches, sausage rolls, crisps, dips, cheeses, or sweet treats. It’s always an absolute feast and a wonderfully relaxed way to catch up with old friends, meet new members, and chat about the weekend ahead over a drink.
Saturday: The Big Gorge Hike & Village Exploring
After breakfast, we’ll head straight out from our accommodation base for our main event:
The Cheddar Gorge Circular
.
We will tackle the dramatic clifftop walk, taking in the breathtaking, rugged views across the Somerset Levels and the Mendip Hills. Keep an eye out for the famous feral goats and Soay sheep that call the gorge home!
Distance:
Approx. 6–8 miles (depending on exact route variations and winter weather conditions).
Difficulty:
Moderate. There are some steep, rocky ascents and descents, but we will take it at a steady group pace.
What to bring:
Sturdy walking boots, warm layers, waterproofs, and a packed lunch.
After the hike, there will be time to explore the charming village of Cheddar, famous for its historic caves, cozy tearooms, and authentic Cheddar cheese. Saturday evening will feature the legendary OutdoorLads group dinner cooked back at our accommodation base.
Sunday: Morning Walk & Departure
We’ll pack up and clear our accommodation by mid-morning, but the fun doesn't have to stop there! For those who want to stick around, we will arrange a shorter, morning walk to conquer nearby Crooks Peak with its dramatic views to the coast and across to Wales before heading home.
Accommodation & Logistics
We are staying at a welcoming, well-equipped base located just a short stroll from the mouth of the gorge itself. It features great spaces to socialise and there's plenty of pubs in Cheddar itself as well.
What to Pack:
Your Friday night buffet contribution, indoor shoes/slippers for the hostel, casual clothes, full hiking gear for Saturday (waterproofs are a must for February!), and towels/toiletries.
Food & Fuel
We’ve got you covered so you can focus on the views:
Included:
Breakfasts on Saturday and Sunday, plus a delicious group dinner on Saturday night.
Tea, Coffee & Cake:
Plenty provided throughout the weekend—because every hiker needs a sugar hit!
Your Part:
Just bring your Friday buffet contribution, your own preferred snacks/drinks, and a packed lunch for Saturday.
Dogs:
Sorry no dogs allowed for this weekend (except registered assistance dogs - please contact the office on
support@outdoorlads.com
when booking)
Closing Date for booking
Please note the closing date for booking onto this event is Sunday 21st Feb at Midday.
Difficulty & Distance: The hikes planned will be roughly a medium difficulty based on distance and weather conditions.

Title: Balcombe Ouse Valley Viaduct Lakeside and Woodland Circular
Summary:
Support Tom on his journey to become an OutdoorLads leader.
This is an
8-mile circular walk
, tailored in duration for a late autumn day. On this walk we’ll head south from Balcombe Station ascending through Wealden woodland before transitioning to the working farmland along the Ouse Valley. We will pass under the awesome Ouse Valley Viaduct, before heading east towards Ardingly Reservoir where we will pause for lunch or snacks, lakeside, weather permitting. We then turn northwards tracing the shoreline enjoying watery vistas across the lake to the body’s north-eastern tip before tracking the mill valley to our second lacustrine treat – Balcombe Lake. Our final ascent takes us back into Balcombe village and the Half Moon Inn, where attendees are welcome to rest and refresh or otherwise head on to Balcombe station or away home by other means.
Here is a link to the
OS map route
Walk highlights
The Viaduct
The Ouse Valley Viaduct, possibly one of the most beautiful feats of Victorian engineering in the British countryside. Completed in 1841, this remarkable railway viaduct carries trains across the River Ouse floodplain near Haywards Heath, supported by 37 elegant brick arches stretching for around 450 metres. Built using approximately 11 million bricks, its curves and classical design make it look almost like a Roman aqueduct rising from the green Sussex landscape. The viaduct was constructed for the London and Brighton Railway, helping to transform travel between the capital and the south coast.
The Lake
Ardlingly Reservoir, created in the 1970s by damming the River Ouse is an important haven for wildlife, attracting a wonderful variety of birds, including herons, grebes and kingfishers, while its reed beds and wooded banks provide shelter for many other species. The reservoir is also popular with sailing and fishing enthusiasts, adding a little activity to what might otherwise seem a wonderfully quiet landscape. As of October 2026, the reservoir has some restricted access due to landslide at its western extent, however the paths to the south and east where we will pass, remain open.
The Village
Balcombe is a historic Sussex village, surrounded by the wooded countryside of the High Weald. The village has medieval roots, and its parish church, St Mary’s, contains elements dating back to the 12th century. Balcombe’s development was greatly influenced by the arrival of the rail travel in 1841, when the London and Brighton Railway arrived. Balcombe has retained some of its traditional village character, with historic buildings, a village green and a close relationship with the surrounding countryside.
Other Information
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks. I just ask that owners please ensure they are kept on a lead as appropriate, especially around livestock and when near busy roads. Please, also remember that not everyone is a dog lover.
This particular walk might have some stiles, so please ensure your dog is comfortable with these.
Don’t Waste That Space!
Walks get filled up quite quickly, so please only sign up if you know you are free to attend.
Plans do sometimes change, but remember to free up your space so someone else can attend.
New Members:
If this is your first event or you are new to OutdoorLads we’d love to see you.
Please message me if you have any questions.
Timings
Whilst every endeavour is made to make the timings of this event accurate, I cannot be guaranteed that we will finish on time and there may be delays.
