Title: Winter Mountaineering in the Cairngorms
Summary:
Cairngorms - Three nights
Winter Mountaineering Weekend for experienced winter mountaineers.
The Cairngorms can be a stunning place to be in winter conditions, with five of the six highest uk mountains, caledonian pine forests and hopefully a little bit of blue sky there should be plenty to aim for. This event is for those with mountaineering experience in winter conditions as you need to be proficient in the use of crampons and ice axes.
The plan for the weekend is to get out onto the mountains for two quality winter mountain days (what we do is very much driven by what the weather is doing!!). This year we are based near Braemar, in the heart of the Cairngorms National Park.
As this weekend involves using crampons and ice axes you may need to hire this equipment along with suitable boots, Ellis Brigham, Nevis Sport and Tiso have selected hire locations in Scotland.
Please remember that this is a winter mountain environment and as such you should have a good level of fitness and be comfortable hiking in challenging terrain, as it is intended that we will be doing mountaineering in snow,
this is not an event for those who don't have suitable experience in winter conditions
. The mountains in the area are generally rounded which reduces the technicality of the activity however the walking will still be challenging, particularly with the distances we will be covering each day. If in doubt please message the event leader for guidance. The exact nature of activities on offer will be dictated by the weather conditions on the day.
Dogs:
This event is not suitable for dogs.

Title: Sheffield January Midweek Social
Summary:

An opportunity for new, regular, and occasional members to meet up. We are generally outdoors kind of guys, but a social is an opportunity for us to catch up over a drink (alcohol or not), and perhaps grab a bite to eat... this venue makes it easy to do both.
Look forward to seeing you.
Is this your first OutdoorLads event?

My First Event
page
.
If you have any other questions you can send a message to the event organiser, whose role is to be welcoming.

Title: Brantingham and the Two Dales
Summary:
Join Chris & Craig for this 9-mile (14.5 km) circular walk from Brantingham in East Yorkshire.
We'll head through the woodlands towards Elloughton Dale, where we'll enjoy sweeping views across the Humber and towards the meeting point of the River Ouse and River Trent. From here, we'll make our way down through Welton Dale, passing the Raikes Mausoleum before arriving in the village of Welton, where we'll stop for lunch with views of the church.
After lunch, there'll be an opportunity to visit the local village pub before we pick up part of the Yorkshire Wolds Way and head towards Turtle Hill. Here, we'll enjoy views across Hull and the surrounding countryside before making our way back to Brantingham.
Your First OutdoorLads Event?
We know that new members in particular like to know in advance more about what an OutdoorLads event will be like.
If this is your first OutdoorLads event, you should check out the information designed specifically for you on the
My First Event
page on the OutdoorLads website.
What if there is a Waiting List?
If this event is fully booked and you want to attend, just add yourself to the waitling list, because places inevitably become available closer to the date.
Want to keep in touch with what's going on in the North East England & Yorkshire Region?
Sign up for the
North East England & Yorkshire Region Telegram Chat Group
, and bookmark our upcoming events list via the short link:
https://outdoorlads.events/northeast
.

All images taken by the event leader with permission for ODL use.

Title: Bouldering MANCHESTER - Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads For An Evening of INDOOR BOULDERING in Manchester!
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Bouldering is a form of climbing that focuses on shorter "problems" emphasising technique, balance, body positioning, and sometimes power, rather than long, high routes. Without the need for ropes, harnesses, and belaying, bouldering is an accessible activity for newcomers and is often considered the "purest" form of climbing.
Bouldering offers a wide range of benefits, including:
Physical:
Improved strength, tone, balance, power, and coordination.
Mental:
Enhanced problem-solving, focus, concentration, and body awareness.
Emotional:
Relaxation, a sense of achievement, and a feeling of mind-body connection.
Bouldering is also a fantastic way to meet new people and build lasting friendships, as it's an inherently social sport where climbers share tips and strategies to conquer the routes.
New to Bouldering?
If you're new to bouldering, it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader to learn the basics of safe bouldering. The leader can then introduce you to the rest of the group where you can refine your newly learnt skills in a social environment.
Experienced Boulderer?
If you’re new to climbing with ODL, the leader will help to introduce you to the rest of the group so you can explore the centre together.
You are responsible for your own safety and actions while bouldering. Please use your own judgement when accepting advice from OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers, regardless of your bouldering experience.
Ready to boulder?
You will need to sign up on the ODL event page. We would ask you to do this each time so that the leader has access to important information
If you are not already registered with Rock Over Climbing, please do so
here
to save time when you arrive. You only need to do this once.
When you arrive at the centre you will need to pay for entry and hire climbing shoes if you don't own a pair. ODL members benefit from the concessionary rate so please mention this when paying.
Get bouldering! You’ll find most of the group already bouldering so feel free to join them. If you’re new to bouldering with ODL, the leader will be looking out for you so if you spot them, please go speak with them first.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.
Photos : Copyright granted to OutdoorLads by
Sieh
and joenellist.
Difficulty & Distance: Suitable for all abilities. If you're new to bouldering, just let the event leader know and we'll get you started!

Title: Indoor Climbing MANCHESTER - Beginners welcome!
Summary:
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Join us for an evening of climbing in one of the UK's top climbing centres. Whether you are new to climbing or a seasoned climber, this centre offers something for everyone with a huge selection of routes including top rope, lead and auto belay.
Prefer to boulder? That's well catered for as well, with an extensive modern bouldering area ensuring there is plenty to keep you busy, or you can swap between climbing and bouldering on the same night.
Climbing is the main focus of the event, but this is also a great chance to meet other members and build lasting friendships. Many Outdoor Lads members join through climbing, so if you're new to the group and want to know more, come along and chat over a cuppa during the tea and cake break.
What to expect on your first climb with us?
If you are an experienced climber and have passed the centre's proficiency test, we'll pair you up with a climbing buddy and you'll be out exploring the centre in no time.
If you have never climbed before or think you could do with a refresher, we offer supervised climbing sessions with one of our leaders, subject to availability. That session will focus on introducing you to climbing, making sure you get plenty of time on the wall whilst also showing you how to belay safely. Due to the centre's rules, we are limited in the number of climbers the leader is able to supervise in each session so if you think you may need a supervised session,
please contact the leader before signing up to make sure there is enough space.
As a general guide, if you answer "no" to any of the following questions, you should opt for a supervised session:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie into a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay and lower down another climber correctly and confidently?
After a few supervised sessions, you should be ready to complete the centre's proficiency test and once that has been passed, you'll be able to climb with the rest of the group.
Everything else you need to know
You will need to register with Big Depot before your first visit to the centre but you only need to do this once. If you are an experienced climber, you can save time and do this online
here
, selecting the 18+ unsupervised option. This also applies if you just want to boulder, just select the relevant options during the registration. If you are a beginner and require a supervised session, the leader will help register you when you are at the centre.
Photos provided by Sieh and Dexmonster.
Difficulty & Distance: There is a range of routes of varying difficulty, but there should be something to suit everybody

Title: Reading Indoor Bouldering
Summary:
This bouldering session presents an ideal opportunity for a fun evening of what I call sociable workout where we take on a wide range of physical (and in fact mental) challenges with the atmosphere always friendly and cheerful. All levels are welcome!
The beauty of bouldering lies in its simplicity: you don't need ropes or a harness, just some climbing shoes which can be hired at the centre and a drive to get the top and overcome some trepidation. It's also a fundamentally social experience, with most of the session spent discussing how to solve particular climbing routes, aka problems, or catching up with each other in between climbs. Bouldering is a great way to get into climbing, come and see what all the fuss is about!
All skill levels are welcome
. If you're new to climbing, we've got you covered with tailored guidance, boosting your skills and confidence while ensuring your safety on and around the wall. Don’t worry about needing to invest in gear before you try. The Climbing Hangar offers
free shoe rentals
so you don’t have to shell out for shoes until you know bouldering is for you.
Experienced boulderer? Dive in and embrace the challenges independently. Just remember to follow the centre's rules for your own safety.
Our ethos is inclusivity. I keep our group tight-knit to foster connection and ensure personalised coaching for everyone, regardless of your experience level. Many climbers started their journeys relatively “late” in life, incl. some session leaders
🤫
We convene at the
Climbing Hangar in Reading
, one of the largest climbing centres in the region. The generously spacious and friendly cafe/lounge is my personal favourite where you can find us socialising, having a cuppa, snacks or even pizza before and after the climbs.
If you have never climbed at the Climbing Hangar in Reading before, you must book an induction slot:
https://www.theclimbinghangar.com/locations/reading
- follow instructions to book an induction slot around the time that this event starts.
You also need to
complete the waiver form that is linked in the confirmation email
once you've booked an induction slot.
This only needs to be done once.

Title: BIRMINGHAM Indoor Climbing - MONDAY - Beginners
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for an evening at Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre.
*** Beginner (supervised) events are not offered every week ***
If you have never climbed before (or need a refresher on the basics), then this BEGINNERS EVENT is ideal for you! We will happily show you the ropes & teach you everything you need to know to climb safely!
Event pages are split into
BEGINNER & EXPERIENCED.
Please ensure you sign up to the correct event as we can only supervise two beginners at once per leader.
This event is for beginner climbers (those needing to be supervised) only!
If you are competent with how to tie in & belay (safely & confidently), then you will need to
sign up to the accompanying experienced (independent climber) event
instead.
If you are climbing with us for the first time, whether Experienced or Beginner, it is essential that you send a note to the Event Leader telling them about your previous climbing experience & your goals!
Bouldering
- Most of us do roped climbing, but if you prefer to do bouldering, you can sign yourself in & go bouldering (unsupervised) instead of, or as well as, roped climbing. Please meet the leader & the group at the start though; some others might wish to do bouldering too!
Please note that we will not teach lead climbing or lead belaying on this event -
we would suggest having some
lessons in Lead Climbing
by a qualified member of staff if this is something you're interested in pursuing!
If you are subsequently unable to attend, please cancel off the event. Spaces for beginners are limited & 'no-shows' are not only rude, but also frustrating for the leader & other attendees who may have travelled over an hour away to climb with you!
Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends & develop your climbing skills.
Climbing
- Unlike Indoor Bouldering there is a certain amount of skill to be mastered, such as tying in knots & belaying a partner, as well as the climbs being higher than in bouldering. If you are new to climbing (or would like a refresher), there are plenty of top-rope routes to choose from after learning the essential climbing & safety techniques with one of our friendly, experienced climbing leaders.
Bouldering
- Instead of tackling long high routes, the 'problems' (as they are referred to) are shorter & focus on technique, balance, body positioning & sometimes power. With the different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, so it’s excellent (but not necessarily easier) for newcomers.
Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
has more than 75 lines with over 300 routes, set through some spectacular ground including its notorious 'stalactite'. It even features one of the few indoor 'Yorkshire VS cracks' in the country, to test your jamming skills. The bouldering rooms are just as interesting as its climbing routes, over 200 bouldering problems have been organised into graded circuits to provide something for everyone.
You MUST register via this event page before coming to the centre!
To climb, you will need to:
Complete a
Registration Form
(please arrive early to do this in-person the first time) & pay a Registration Fee:
Annual Registration
is
£5
or
Day Registration
is
£3
Pay an
Entry Fee
directly to the climbing centre:
Standard Entry
is
£12.50
&
Bouldering Only
is
£8.50.
Hire
climbing shoes (
£3.50
) & a climbing harness (
£3.50
) if you don't own your own.
Please see Redpoint's
website
for current prices & note that prices are subject to change.
If you have any questions or need any more information just get in touch with the event leader by clicking on their profile below, or take a look at the
My first climbing event page
for more information.
PLEASE NOTE:
All those attending the event must also be aware of the climbing centre's own terms & conditions of participation & abide by them, along with any instructions given by the centre's staff.

taken & used with permission of
R. Casabuena
&
K. Jones
.
Difficulty & Distance: This event is for BEGINNER (supervised) climbers only!!!

Title: A Festive Monumental Winter Wander
Summary:
Join the group for an exploration of the lower River Wear and a climb up to Penshaw Monument to take in the views from this vantage point often glimpsed when on a journey up the A19 or from a distance on several popular hikes on the coast.
This walk uses well established and signed paths and bridleways to cover distance pretty easily with one short steeper climb and quick descent to visit the historic outstanding piece of architecture, loved by those locally and very well admired by visitors.
This imposing structure was built to honour John George Lambton the first Earl of Durham and was completed in 1845 and is in the care of the National Trust.  The epic seventy foot high monument stands proudly on the summit of Penshaw Hill and is said to be a replica of the Temple of Hephaetus in Athens.  It is known very well by football fans as this appear on the badge of Sunderland Football Club.
As it is winter the intention is to stop half way at a public house for some warm food and to reheat, we will also be stopping for snacks along the way.
This walk has always proved popular with members and it demonstrates the best of the Northeast area where countryside sandwiched between towns and cities can also offer scenic gems, great woodland stretches and river views.
Come along and join the leader Steven for a great Wearside Wander as the year of 2026 draws to a close.
This walk is suitable for dogs , our four legged friends will also enjoy this day out.

Title: Helsby Hill and Frodsham Woods
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a scenic hike along the Cheshire Sandstone Ridge, taking in dramatic hilltop views, ancient history, rich woodland ecology and a wander through one of Cheshire’s most attractive historic parks.
Points of interest on the route
Helsby Hill & Hill Fort
Helsby Hill is one of the most striking landmarks on the Sandstone Ridge, rising above the Cheshire countryside and offering superb views across the Mersey Estuary and into Wales. Near the summit are the remains of an Iron Age hillfort, with clear ramparts and earthworks that once defended a prominent settlement. It’s a short, steep climb, but the views and history make it well worth the effort.
The Sandstone Trail
We’ll follow a section of the Sandstone Trail, a 55km long‑distance path running from Frodsham to Whitchurch. This part of the trail offers ancient wooded slopes, rocky outcrops and wide views over the Cheshire Plain. It’s a great way to experience the varied landscapes of the Mid Cheshire Ridge.
Frodsham Woods
Frodsham Woods form a large, connected area of broadleaved woodland, meadows and regenerating habitats above the town. Thousands of native trees have been planted here in recent years, creating a rich habitat for wildlife. Buzzards, badgers, foxes and a variety of butterflies and woodland birds are commonly seen, and the mix of old and new woodland makes this a particularly interesting area to explore.
Castle Park House & Gardens
Towards the end of the walk we’ll pass through this lovely historic park with formal lawns, wooded areas, sculptures and a restored Victorian conservatory. It’s a peaceful spot to stop for a break before completing the final leg back to Helsby and well earned beer.
Other Information
Dog Suitability
Dogs are always welcome on my walks, though their behaviour and safety is their owner’s responsibility. This includes cleaning up after them, controlling their behaviour around other animals or people, and assisting them over any stiles or streams we may cross.
New Members
We know that new members in particular like to know in advance more about what an OutdoorLads event will be like. If this is your first OutdoorLads event, you should check out the
My First Event
page on the OutdoorLads website.

Title: Duffield to Derby - DVH Way Section 7
Summary:
The Derwent Valley Trust
was set up in 1996 to promote the history, arts, wildlife and leisure opportunities that surround the river Derwent along its 55 mile course through Derbyshire.
The Derwent Valley Heritage Way
takes us from Ladybower Reservoir in the Peak District National Park to its end at Derwent Mouth where it flows into the River Trent near Shardlow.
The route is divided into eight sections of between  ~13 km (8 miles) and ~17 km (10.5 miles), each with a clear public transport solution. All, except the first section, are linear routes. We park at the end, travel to the start, and walk back to our cars. Sections 5, 6, 7 are brilliantly served by the East Midlands Railway Derwent Valley Line
(Derby–Matlock, hourly), which runs almost parallel to the trail the whole way. For sections (2, 3, 4 and 8), we use local buses.
Each section is a walk in itself. Join one or more, as you wish, or walk all eight sections to complete the whole route through Derbyshire. Please ask other attendees for a lift if you need one.
Section 7 – Duffield to Derby ~13.5 km (8.4 miles) Total ascent 92 m (302 ft)
From the station we make a slight detour to visit the site of
Duffield Castle
occupied by Henry de Ferrers, Duchy of Lancaster soon after the Norman Conquest. He owned hunting grounds nearby known as Duffield Frith.
We walk through Duffield, over towards St Alkmund's Church, and cross over the river at Duffield Bridge.
Peckwash Mill
, built in 1805, became one of the biggest paper mills in the country during the mid nineteenth century. Its spectacular chimney was added in 1895 but the emission of smoke upset a neighbour that led to the demise of the business.
Stone from the nearby
Rigga Quarry
area was used in the construction of Derby Cathedral and other notable buildings around the Midlands.
We pass through Little Eaton and follow the Derwent towards Darley Abbey where
The Evans' family Boar's Head Mill
enabled a huge expansion of the village at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution.
We walk through Darley Park to Little Chester, the oldest area of Derby, once occupied by Romans who called their fort,
Derventio
.
During the late 19th century,
Alfred Seale Haslam
pioneered the production of dry-air refrigeration equipment used to import frozen food from Australia and South America. He built many of the houses around Chester Green for his workforce. By 1891 he was Mayor of Derby and received Queen Victoria for a state visit.
We head over Handyside Bridge, which used to carry the
Great Northern Railway
line, a rival to the Midland Railway.
We pass
St Mary's Bridge Chapel
to Derby City of Making museum housed in the original Lombe's Mill that employed some 300 people at its height, in effect, the world’s first modern factory.
The route passes the back of the Council House and continues through the Bass Recreation Ground to Culvert Street, a conservation area of traditional terraced houses built by the Midland Railway.
At the end of the walk there an opportunity to visit the Brunswick pub near to the station.
Well behaved
dogs are welcome
but must kept under control at all times.

Title: Arise from your Stupor for a Super-Duper Trooper Looper!
Summary:
Stupor
(noun)
:
a lack of critical mental function; for instance, that brought about by festive overindulgence.
Super-Duper
(adjective, informal)
:
extremely good; for instance, Ashford Hangers and Shoulder of Mutton Hill in Hampshire.
Trooper
(noun): a private soldier, or an uncomplaining and persevering person; for instance, a member of the GBTQ outdoor activity charity OutdoorLads; also the name of an inn in said area of Hampshire, where said members have a private luncheon booking.
Looper
(noun)
:
a person or thing that makes loops; for instance, the route said members will follow around said area, mostly on tarmac lanes and starting and ending at Petersfield Railway Station.
The sights:
Ashford Hangers - Shoulder of Mutton Hill:
In his
England's Hundred Best Views,
Simon Jenkins regards the vista from Shoulder of Mutton Hill as one of nation's finest. He writes: 'In the distance we can see the long ridge of the South Downs floating comfortably across the horizon. To the south the contour softens towards the coast at Portsmouth. But above the village of Steep the hills seem to lose all discipline. The greensand ridges of the Hampshire Downs argue with each other. Escarpments bunch and jostle. Beech woods cling to the slopes in dramatic clumps known as hangers...The area is known from its contours as Little Switzerland, though Little Tuscany might be more appropriate'. Evoked and mythologised by local poet Edward Thomas, we'll see his monument at the viewpoint.
Ashford Hangers - Cobbett's View:
The journalist, politician and social reformer William Cobbett described the view from Wheatham Hill in November 1822 thus: “... out we came, all in a moment, at the very edge of the hanger! And never, in all my life, was I so surprised and so delighted! I pulled up my horse, and sat and looked; and it was like looking from the top of a castle down into the sea, except that the valley was land and not water.”
High Cross:
A spacious, scattered flint and chalk village high up on the plateau behind Stoner Hill and Shoulder of Mutton Hill. At an altitude of 200 metres above sea level, among the highest villages in Hampshire. Possesses a fine late-Victorian church.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them. It is of moderate length, but there will be fields with livestock and a number of stiles and roads to negotiate and lanes to walk along. A dog must be obedient if it is off the lead.
The
route
(please click the link to see the route at the Ordnance Survey website):
Heading west along the A272 Winchester Road and crossing under the A3, we'll turn north at Stroud and proceed up lanes towards Lythe Hanger which we'll ascend. At Ridge Top Lane we'll turn west, then north, then east to reach Froxfield Green. Then, following lanes north and east we'll hit High Cross. Lanes heading further east will take us to the crossing of the main road at The Trooper Inn. We'll then find Old Litten Lane which will bring us to Ashford Hangers and the viewpoints. Descending Wheatham Hill, we'll follow lanes heading to Steep where we'll pick up the Hangers Way which will take us back to Petersfield.

Title: Lost Tracks, Green Chain, an Oak & Screaming Alice!
Summary:
'Screaming Alice' was Cockney rhyming slang for Crystal Palace!
This
linear walk
takes you from the historic streets and leafy cemetery surroundings of
Nunhead, Honor Oak and Sydenham
through the green corridors of south-east London, and along the traces of the long-lost
Crystal Palace High Level railway
.
Following sections of the
Green Chain Walk
, it combines woodland paths, quiet residential streets,
local history
and the remnants of a railway that once carried visitors towards the magnificent
Crystal
Palace
. We will also have time to enjoy the recently reopened Crystal Palace
museum and the park
.
The highlights
Camberwell Old Cemetery
: includes a Zeppelin Raid Memorial honoring 21 civilians killed during a First World War German air raid in 1917.
One Tree Hill
: not the US TV show, but a lovely spot for views across London. The hill's
Oak of Honor
(which gives its name to the local area Honor Oak) once marked the southern boundary of the Norman Honour of Gloucester. According to legend, Queen Elizabeth I rested under an oak at the summit on her way to visit Lewisham in 1602. The current oak is the third on the site, planted in 1905.
The Great North Wood and Sydenham Hill Wood:
Together with Dulwich Wood, Sydenham Hill Wood makes up the largest remaining fragment of the Great North Wood. It is managed by London Wildlife Trust and is a patchwork of ancient woodland, that covers the old railway trackbed.
Horniman Museum & Gardens
: We'll briefly stop here for lunch and to enjoy the views. Note there wont be time to visit the museum.
The Crystal Palace and South London Junction Railway
: Also known as the Crystal Palace High Level branch line opened in 1865 from Nunhead with stations at Honor Oak, Lordship Lane, Upper Sydenham and Crystal Palace High Level. Following the destruction of the Crystal Palace by fire in 1936, the line lost most of its original function of carrying visitors to events in the Palace. Manpower shortages led to a second closure from 1944 to 1946. When services were reintroduced they were very lightly used, and the line finally closed on 20 September 1954. The track was lifted in 1956 and all the stations, but one, were demolished. The northern part remains in use as part of the former Greenwich Park branch line and the Catford Loop Line.
Crystal Palace Museum
: This small free volunteer led Museum is only open on Fridays and Sundays. It tells the story of the mighty Crystal Palace from its Hyde Park origins to Sydenham Hill, which later took the name Crystal Palace, and fire which destroyed it in 1936. A friend of mine is a volunteer at the museum and may be able to give us an overview of the Palace history.
Crystal Palace Park:
We finish among the historic landscape and far reaching views, Italian terraces, sphinx and famous Victorian dinosaur sculptures. There's also a visitor centre in the park.
The route
You can view the route in OS Maps
here
.
Dogs

I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them. Please abide by the
Countryside Code
and also remember not everyone loves dogs as much as you do, so please be mindful of other members.
Afterwards
We'll grab a drink in a nearby pub.
New members
New members are always welcome. Please message me in advance if you have any questions before the walk.

Title: A Wild Night In: A Celebration of Mountaineering
Summary:
Mountains have always been a source of fascination - inspiring both fear and awe in equal measure. And the stories of those who seek to climb them have become modern folklore - compelling tales of tragedy, survival, high stakes and human achievement.
A Wild Night In celebrates many of the most momentous and inspiring stories in the history of mountaineering seen through the RSGS archive. Hear in person from some of the world’s leading climbers, including Leo Houlding, Dave MacLeod, Polly Murray and Louise Flockhart, alongside other notable guests - offering a unique opportunity to hear so many remarkable figures from the world of climbing, all in one evening. An evening of inspiration plus an opportunity to ask your own questions.

Title: Humps & Bumps of the Clent Hills
Summary:
Hill Walk: 8 miles, 383m ascent. Autumn woods and fabulous views!
(This walk was postponed from 24 October due to weather)
Booking now reopened-apologies for it being closed due to postponement.
Welcome to a new series of walks exploring the humps and bumps of the Central region! Humps are hills with more than 100 metres prominence, and bumps are bulges which protrude a little less. You can find out more about humps
here
. Expect one or two quips on the way round!
The Clent Hills include Walton Hill, at 315m a prominent Hump. Our route begins at Nimmings Wood car park, from where we ascend gradually to the Four Stones viewpoint. The stones look like something from prehistoric times, but were actually erected in the 1750s by Lord Lyttleton of Hagley Hall. The view from here is outstanding on a clear day, particularly to the South West, all the way to the Malverns, Cotswolds and even the Brecon Beacons.
Passing Clent Hill 309m, we descend then ascend the second of the main summits which is slightly higher, Walton Hill at 315m. This is our Hump for today! Walton Hill has fine views especially East towards the Birmingham skyline. Views continue as we follow the top of the ridge south to Calcot Hill, then take the track west.
The woods here include fine, historic woodland and traditional species, particularly oaks, beech, birch and hazel, and a wide variety of fungi in autumn. You may see deer hiding in the woods too!
Lunch stop is just over half way at the top of Clent village. Here, there is a grassy slope good for picnics, the Four Stones café and the Hill Tavern. We are 1 mile from the car park here, so if you wish to take a short cut back that is possible.
In the afternoon, we tackle a bump. A gentle, ancient track takes us to Hagley, where we cross the main road and ascend Wychbury Hill, a bump. It is a fine bump with an obelisk on the top. There are prominent views back over Clent and across Worcestershire.
This is a hill walk with good paths, totally 8 miles with 383m ascent. Find the route
here
. Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk. If you have any questions, please send the event leader a message.

Title: Glasgow climbing - beginners welcome!
Summary:
Come and join ODL for weekly evening climbing at the Glasgow Climbing Centre. Whether this is your first experience of climbing or a pro, this venue has something for everyone.
This event is for members of all levels of experience and ability and all are welcome to come along.
The cost is the standard entry fee to the centre. Informal tuition will also be able from OutdoorLads, but this is dependent on numbers.
Climbing is a total body workout. It is not just about strength, but requires balance, problem solving and planning. Climbing routes are like puzzles that might need some breaking down, planning or practice. Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends and develop your climbing skills.
Founded in 1994, The Glasgow Climbing Centre was one of the first dedicated indoor climbing gyms in Scotland. Today it is the largest indoor roped climbing centre in the West of Scotland and the preferred training facility for many new and experienced climbers.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
Yes! Beginners are very welcome. If you've never climbed before, just let us know by messaging the event leader, so we can arrange for you to be signed into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try. If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely.
What other Climbing events do OutdoorLads Run?
We run regular indoor climbing and bouldering events across the UK. We are always keen to put more on, so if you fancy climbing in your local area contact a climbing leader and we can see what we can arrange.

Title: Glasgow climbing - beginners welcome!
Summary:
Come and join ODL for weekly evening climbing at the Glasgow Climbing Centre. Whether this is your first experience of climbing or a pro, this venue has something for everyone.
This event is for members of all levels of experience and ability and all are welcome to come along.
The cost is the standard entry fee to the centre. Informal tuition will also be able from OutdoorLads, but this is dependent on numbers.
Climbing is a total body workout. It is not just about strength, but requires balance, problem solving and planning. Climbing routes are like puzzles that might need some breaking down, planning or practice. Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends and develop your climbing skills.
Founded in 1994, The Glasgow Climbing Centre was one of the first dedicated indoor climbing gyms in Scotland. Today it is the largest indoor roped climbing centre in the West of Scotland and the preferred training facility for many new and experienced climbers.

Title: Barny Winter Wander
Summary:
Join Steven for a rewarding walk beside the River Tees in rural County Durham as the light fades and winter takes a bite.
The route is a fairly unchallenging wander on bridleways, narrow footpaths and over pasture in an area of picturesque villages , beautiful riverside woodlands with far reaching views towards the high Pennines.
The hike takes advantage in the most part of a well signed long distance path - the Teesdale Way, the initial stage though highlights an interesting deep side valley of atmospheric woodland and passes under an old disused railway viaduct.  On the route there is much evidence of the old railways that were long ago abandoned.
A couple of miles wind across farmland to a steep elevated section above the river that takes us to where two rivers meet and an excellent tranquil spot for a winter picnic.
Then at an easy pace the afternoon will follow the River Tees downstream with another short diversion to another side valley to finish with the iconic view of the castle ruins ahead.
Wrap up warm, put your winter hiking boots on and please join us for a great festive day in the gem of a location.

Difficulty & Distance: Medium distance, gradual ascents, one steep short slope down 14.9km 10.25mile

Title: Wildfell - Walking in the footsteps of Anne Brontë
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a classic 7 mile/11K walk out in the heart of West Yorkshire’s Brontë Country! Starting in the famous cobbled village of Haworth, we’ll head out across wild heather moors, visit picturesque cascades, and explore the rugged landscapes that inspired Anne, Charlotte, and Emily Brontë.
​Whether you’re a big fan of literary history or just looking for a brilliant hike with a friendly group of guys, this walk delivers stunning Pennine views, fresh moorland air, and a warm welcome. The route is a mix of cobbled streets, stone-pitched paths, uneven moorland tracks, and open hillsides (can get muddy in spots!)
Whilst not part of this event this weekend also sees Haworth celebrating its
Torchlight procession
so, if you wish, you can enjoy a Magical Christmas in Historic Haworth joining the throng to march up Main Street behind the flaming torches, singing at every stop - or you can pick a good spot on the sidelines and catch the procession as it passes
​
What to Expect
​
Historic Haworth Village:
Meet on the famous cobbled Main Street, passing the historic Brontë Parsonage and old churchyard before setting off.
​
Brontë Falls & Brontë Bridge:
Stroll through the valley to the scenic stone cascades and natural rock pools where the sisters often walked and wrote.
​
Open Moorland Trails:
Climb through Penistone Hill Country Park and out onto the open, windswept heather moors.
​
Top Withens Ruin:
Reach the famous ruined moorland farmhouse tied to the literary history of
Wuthering Heights
, offering panoramic views back down the Worth Valley.
​
Reservoir Return:
Loop back via peaceful waterside tracks around Lower Laithe Reservoir.
​
Pub Finish:
Head back down Haworth's cobbles for a well-earned post-walk pint or warm drink in one of the village's cozy local pubs!
If the event is fully booked:
Please join the waiting list as people frequently drop out during the week before an event, and you are likely to get a place on the walk.
If this is your first OutdoorLads walk event,
we’ll make sure you feel welcome. Please
check out the My First Event page
, and don’t hesitate to drop me a message if you have questions or want to know more about this walk.

Title: Bouldering NORTH WALES - Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads For An Evening of INDOOR BOULDERING in NORTH WALES!
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Bouldering is a form of climbing that focuses on shorter "problems" emphasising technique, balance, body positioning, and sometimes power, rather than long, high routes. Without the need for ropes, harnesses, and belaying, bouldering is an accessible activity for newcomers and is often considered the "purest" form of climbing.
Bouldering offers a wide range of benefits, including:
Physical:
Improved strength, tone, balance, power, and coordination.
Mental:
Enhanced problem-solving, focus, concentration, and body awareness.
Emotional:
Relaxation, a sense of achievement, and a feeling of mind-body connection.
Bouldering is also a fantastic way to meet new people and build lasting friendships, as it's an inherently social sport where climbers share tips and strategies to conquer the routes.
New to Bouldering?
If you're new to bouldering, it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader to learn the basics of safe bouldering. The leader can then introduce you to the rest of the group where you can refine your newly learnt skills in a social environment.
Experienced Boulderer?
If you’re new to climbing with ODL, the leader will help to introduce you to the rest of the group so you can explore the centre together.
You are responsible for your own safety and actions while bouldering. Please use your own judgement when accepting advice from OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers, regardless of your bouldering experience.
Ready to boulder?
You will need to sign up on the ODL event page. We would ask you to do this each time so that the leader has access to important information
If you are not already registered with The Boardroom Climbing centre you will need to do so when you arrive. Maybe arrive a little earlier to do so.
When you arrive at the centre you will need to pay for entry and hire climbing shoes if you don't own a pair.
Get bouldering! You’ll find most of the group already bouldering so feel free to join them. If you’re new to bouldering with ODL, the leader will be looking out for you so if you spot them, please go speak with them first.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.
Photos : Copyright granted to OutdoorLads by Mark Mckee
Difficulty & Distance: Suitable for all abilities. If you're new to bouldering, just let the event leader know and we'll get you started!

Title: Brighton: Burning The Clocks 2026
Summary:
For three decades now, Burning the Clocks has been a special date in Brighton’s calendar. Taking place on the winter solstice, this magical, unique procession brings wonder to the streets, with a stream of luminous lanterns and a spectacular 2,000-strong parade.
For photos and info see the
organiser's website.
Burning the clocks relies on crowd support to make sure the event happens every year and due to low funding the event did not happen in 2025 Please consider donating by contactless payment on the night or via the website link above cash is also accepted.
When the winter carnival has wound its way to the beach, people pass their handmade paper and willow lanterns – filled symbolically with their hopes and dreams – into a blazing bonfire and prepare for the spectacular fire show and firework display.
Held on the shortest day (longest night) of the year, this growing tradition marks the passing of time by ‘burning the clocks’ and welcoming in the new sun. With over 20,000 spectators, this popular event turns the spotlight away from the more commercial side of Christmas and lights up the darkest of winter nights.
After the parade finishes we will proceed to the popular Legends bar on Brighton’s seafront to watch the fireworks from the balcony and for Decembers Social.
Photos taken by Outdoor Lads member Cassidyi with permission for Outdoor Lads use.

Title: Manchester History, Art and Christmas Markets walk 2026
Summary:
An easy walk around Manchester city centre finding out a bit of Manchester’s history, discovering some great works of art and finishing at the Christmas markets or Manchester's Gay village.
We will meet in the centre of Manchester and see the Central Library, the Town Hall and Midland Hotel.
We will start by visiting the statue of Abraham Lincoln and finding out how the American Civil War affected the cotton industry in the north west.
We will then visit the site of the Peterloo Massacre when a peaceful protest for equality and democracy was broken up with force and 18 people killed.
We will then visit the City Art Gallery for a lightning tour of some great pictures, in particular work by the Pre-Raphaelite painters Waterhouse, Madox Brown and Holman Hunt.
We will finish with a visit to Sackville Park in the heart of the Gay Village and see the memorial to Alan Turing.
There will then be an opportunity to visit the Christmas markets or have a drink or two in Manchester's Gay village.

Title: Sunrise on Snowdon
Summary:
Snowdon Sunrise – A Sea of Clouds?
Watching the sun rise from the summit of Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa), the highest mountain in Wales, is a truly special experience. And at this time of year, we have the added possibility of witnessing a temperature inversion.
A temperature inversion occurs when the air is warmer higher up a mountain than it is lower down — the opposite of what normally happens. Cold air becomes trapped in valleys and hollows, while warmer air sits above it. When conditions are just right, this creates one of the most spectacular sights in the UK mountains: a sea of cloud or mist filling the valleys, with mountain summits rising above it into clear skies and sunshine.
Imagine watching the first rays of sunlight spread across this incredible landscape from the very top of Wales. Magical! Of course, there's no guarantee we'll get an inversion, but fingers crossed.
We'll set off from Llanberis in the darkness and make our way up the Llanberis Path, the most gradual and accessible route to the summit. With our head torches lighting the way, we'll wind our way steadily up the mountainside beneath a star-filled sky, hopefully arriving at the summit just as the sun begins to appear over the horizon.
After taking in the sunrise, enjoying the views and bagging the summit cairn, we'll begin our descent, taking a short detour off the main path to complete our return to Llanberis.
Fitness and experience
This is a challenging mountain walk, not a stroll in the park! The Llanberis Path is approximately 7.25 km each way, with around 975 metres of ascent. We'll be walking in darkness, potentially in freezing temperatures and exposed mountain conditions, so a good standard of fitness, suitable equipment and a positive attitude are essential.
Winter weather on Snowdon can be severe, with snow, ice and strong winds possible. This event will be weather-dependent, and the route or plans may need to change if conditions are unsuitable. Please come prepared for a proper winter mountain adventure!
Event full?
Please join the waiting list. Places usually open up as the event gets nearer and, where necessary, we try to add additional leaders to increase the numbers, so you are highly likely to get a place.

Title: Chilterns Christmas Caper – Bank Holiday Burn-Off
Summary:
Please note that this event is taking place on a Monday (bank holiday) over the Christmas holiday period.
Overview:
🥾
Time to get out of the Christmas closet… and into the countryside!
Back for another Chilterns Christmas caper! Having explored this area last Christmas, we’re back with a different route, more winter countryside and a few festive treats along the way. Expect picture-postcard villages, a touch of TV magic, a dramatic Thames weir and a well-earned pub stop. With the Chilterns and Thames valley either looking their seasonal best (or drab and dreary worst!) it's still the perfect excuse to escape the Christmas home chaos, stretch your legs and enjoy some fresh air with good company. 🍻🎄
Waitlist
: If this event becomes fully booked, but if you'd like to attend,
please add yourself to the waitlist.
For this walk I am planning a medium group size of up to 15 to 20, recognising that train travel out of London is not feasible.
The Route:
With limited daylight, we’ll make an early 10am start, aiming to be back in Henley before dusk.
From Henley-on-Thames railway station, we’ll head towards the river for views of the bridge before passing through the town centre along Hart Street. At the edge of town, near Fairmile, we’ll join the Oxfordshire Way and climb out of the valley into Henley Park. A lovely stretch through parkland follows, before country lanes take us through Fawley and into the extensive woodland of Great Wood. We’ll then descend towards the picturesque village of Hambleden, where we’ll stop for lunch.
After lunch, we’ll follow footpaths across fields alongside the Hamble Brook chalk stream, before crossing the main road at Mill End. One of the highlights comes next: crossing the River Thames via its impressive weir towards Hambleden Lock, where the rush of fast water can be particularly spectacular in the winter after wet weather.
From the lock, we’ll head uphill to the hamlet of Aston, with the tempting option of a refreshment stop at the Flower Pot Inn. Suitably refreshed, we’ll continue along country lanes towards Remenham before completing our return to Henley. Depending on ground conditions, our final stretch will either follow the riverside or take the lane back into town.
The route can be found
here
:
The Sites:
Henley-on-Thames:
is an elegant, historic market town nestled beside the River Thames at the edge of the Chiltern Hills. Globally renowned for its rowing heritage and the iconic Royal Regatta, it features a beautiful waterfront and a vibrant town centre rich in Georgian architecture.
Hambleden:
is one of England’s prettiest villages, its timeless streets are lined with historic brick-and-flint cottages, a 14th-century church, and a classic village pump. It frequently serves as a backdrop for cinematic and television period dramas. It's location in a valley with the Hamble Brook chalk stream passing through it is framed by rolling farmland and ancient beech woodland.
Hambleden Lock and Weir:
form one of the most dramatic and historic engineering landmarks along the Thames Path. First built as a pound lock in 1773, this site marks the historic starting stretch of the very first Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race in 1829. Today, hikers can cross directly over the rushing, churning waters via an impressive 19th-century public footbridge that spans the massive concrete weir. The crossing offers panoramic, photogenic views of the river, the iconic Grade II listed Hambleden Mill, and the surrounding Chiltern hills.
The Flower Pot:
is a characterful late-Victorian country pub and boutique inn built in 1890, tucked away in the peaceful hamlet of Aston.
Dogs:
Well-behaved dogs are welcome, there will be a few areas where we are walking along or crossing roads but the majority of the walk is in open countryside where dogs can be let off the lead. Please abide by the Countryside Code (
https://tinyurl.com/rlqvp3h
) and remember not everyone loves dogs as much as you do so be mindful of other members.
Photos:
All photos the leader's own (taken at different times of the year so not necessarily representative of conditions late December), with permission given to OutdoorLads for use.
Difficulty & Distance: 10.5 miles (17 km) hike, primarily on well-maintained paths and lanes,  which may have some traffic.  Some sections may be muddy. The route includes some moderate hills with an elevation gain of 220 meters

Title: Boots, Beacon and Beer Walk
Summary:
Glynde & Firle Beacon Craft Beer Circular
Starting and finishing in
Glynde, East Sussex
, near Lewes, this circular walk is perfect for OutdoorLads who enjoy a good hike, spectacular South Downs scenery and a well-earned craft beer at the end!
Join us for a
small, friendly and intimate group walk
as we head out from Glynde and climb onto the South Downs. The walk gets off to a challenging start with a steep ascent, but the effort is soon rewarded with
stunning panoramic views across the Sussex countryside
.
We’ll make our way towards
Firle Beacon
, standing at 217 metres, taking in the rolling chalk hills, open downland and beautiful views along the way. We’ll also pass close to the impressive
Firle Place
, before completing our circular route back towards Glynde.
And, of course, no OutdoorLads walk for craft beer lovers would be complete without a
proper pub finale
! We finish the walk back at Glynde Train Station, home to the Steamworks Bar, where we can enjoy a few well-earned craft beers and swap stories from the day.
🥾 Walk highlights
Stunning South Downs views
– especially spectacular on a clear day
Firle Beacon
– climb to the 217m summit
Beautiful Sussex countryside
– rolling hills, chalk downs and picturesque villages
Firle Place
– one of the area's historic country estates
Challenging opening climb
– earn those views!
Craft beer pub finale
– the perfect reward after a day on the Downs 🍻
Bring your walking boots, plenty of water and your thirst for adventure...
Check out the route on
OS Maps
.
After the walk
The fun doesn’t have to end when the walking stops! We’ll head to Glynde Steamworks Bar at the railway station to enjoy a few well-earned pints and continue the good company. If you fancy some food afterwards, you can hop on the train into Lewes, where you’ll find a much wider choice of pubs, restaurants and places to grab a bite to eat.
Further Information

The Guardian 10 of the best railway station pubs in England
.

Title: Indoor Climbing NORTH WALES - Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads For An Evening of INDOOR CLIMBING in NORTH WALES!
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Join us for an evening of indoor climbing! Whether you are new to climbing or a seasoned climber, this centre offers something for everyone with a huge selection of routes.
While
climbing
will be the main focus of the event, the centre offer great
bouldering
problems too, so if that's more you're thing, then you're more than welcome to come along and just boulder. But this is also a great chance to meet other members and build lasting friendships. Many OutdoorLads members join through climbing, so if you're new to the group and want to know more, come along and chat over a cuppa during the tea and cake break.
What to expect on your first climb with us?
If you are an experienced climber and have passed the centre's proficiency test, we'll pair you up with a climbing buddy and you'll be out exploring the centre in no time.
If you have never climbed before or think you could do with a refresher, we offer supervised climbing sessions with one of our leaders, subject to availability. That session will focus on introducing you to climbing, making sure you get plenty of time on the wall whilst also showing you how to belay safely. Due to the centre's rules, we are limited in the number of climbers the leader is able to supervise in each session so if you think you may need a supervised session,
please contact the leader before signing up to make sure there is enough space.
As a general guide, if you answer "no" to any of the following questions, you will need to be supervised for the session:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie into a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay and lower down another climber correctly and confidently?
After a few supervised sessions, you should be ready to complete the centre's proficiency test and once that has been passed, you'll be able to climb with the rest of the group.
Everything else you need to know
You will need to register with
The Boardroom Climbing centre
before you start climbing. You only need to do this once and can be done on the day. This also applies if you just want to boulder, just select the relevant options during the registration. If you are a beginner and require a supervised session, the leader will help register you when you are at the centre.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.

Difficulty & Distance: There is a range of routes of varying difficulty, but there should be something to suit everybody

If you have never climbed before or think you could do with a refresher, we offer supervised climbing sessions with one of our leaders, subject to availability. That session will focus on introducing you to climbing, making sure you get plenty of time on the wall whilst also showing you how to belay safely. Due to the centre's rules, we are limited in the number of climbers the leader is able to supervise in each session so if you think you may need a supervised session,
please contact the leader before signing up to make sure there is enough space.
As a general guide, if you answer "no" to any of the following questions, you will need to be supervised for the session:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie into a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay and lower down another climber correctly and confidently?
After a few supervised sessions, you should be ready to complete the centre's proficiency test and once that has been passed, you'll be able to climb with the rest of the group.
Everything else you need to know
You will need to register with
The Boardroom Climbing centre
before you start climbing. You only need to do this once and can be done on the day. This also applies if you just want to boulder, just select the relevant options during the registration. If you are a beginner and require a supervised session, the leader will help register you when you are at the centre.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.

After a loop north of the Country Park we will head past a hotel and site of a popular summer festival and into the public park.  This area has seen huge improvements to when the walk leader first came here as a child.
We will walk around the larger lake and then to an impressive folly on the top of a rise giving a good panorama of the entire walk area today.
After joining a path around the Serpentine pools we will visit the café before the final short section to the town centre where we could stop to have a drink and hot food.
This walk is suitable for well behaved dogs, these should be kept under close control when near the many geese and ducks.
Please join Steven as he returns to the place he regularly visited as a young one many decades ago.

We’ll start with a nostalgic trip on the historic East Lancashire Heritage Railway from Bury to Ramsbottom, before heading out on a scenic circuit packed with iconic views, heritage, and great company.
Whether you're a regular or joining us for your very first OutdoorLads event, this walk offers a great mix of rolling countryside, wild moorland, and rich local history—a perfect day out to catch up with friends and meet new ones.
What to Expect
Historic Railway Journey: Kick off the day aboard the nostalgic East Lancashire Railway from Bury to Ramsbottom, enjoying scenic autumnal views along the Irwell Valley.
Riverside Stroll: Follow the peaceful path along the River Irwell, enjoying gentle waterside walking as we head toward the hills.
Stubbins Estate & Woodlands: Wander down through the beautiful autumnal woods and countryside paths of the National Trust Stubbins Estate.
Holcombe Moor Trek: Experience the open, fresh air of Holcombe Moor with scenic high-ground trails.
Peel Tower & Panoramic Vistas: Head up Holcombe Hill to the landmark Peel Tower for sweeping, spectacular views across Manchester, the West Pennines, and beyond.

Title: No Footslog to the Spotted Dog - Another Kentish Castles Christmas Cracker
Summary:
A wintry Wealden walk where Yuletide cheer meets Tudor charm. We’ll visit Chiddingstone, one of England’s best-preserved Tudor villages, with its timber-framed houses and cobbled pavement, before crossing the lakeside grounds of Chiddingstone Castle, a Gothic-revival mansion. Footpaths and country lanes will then lead us through gentle farmland towards Smarts Hill, where we'll eat in the private dining room of The Spotted Dog pub. We’ll continue to Penshurst, whose magnificent medieval manor, Penshurst Place, has become the epitome of Elizabethan evocativeness. All in all, we might not be walking in a winter wonderland, but the band of brothers bonhomie will be brilliant.
The sights:
Chiddingstone:
A unique and perfect example of a Tudor one-street village, so perfect, that the whole place is in the care of the National Trust. It's quite a film star too, as it featured in the 1985 Merchant Ivory film
A Room With a View,
Michael Winner's 1983
The Wicked Lady
and the outdoor scenes of the BBC's 1971
Elizabeth R
, starring Glenda Jackson. St Mary's Church is opulent, C14 and C15, and has the tombs to the Streatfeild family (you may have heard of Noel, the author) who lived at early C19 Chiddingstone Castle. The village takes its name from the Chiding Stone, a Saxon judicial place or boundary marker and place of public correction or 'chiding'.
Penshurst:
The village occupies a sheltered position in the rolling Weald, its historic core clustered around the parish church and the approach to Penshurst Place. It retains a notably coherent group of timber-framed houses, cottages and later brick buildings, many with steeply pitched tiled roofs and projecting upper storeys. St John the Baptist’s church, set back from the street, is principally medieval, with C13 and C14 arcades and a fine Perpendicular west tower; its Victorian restoration was by George Gilbert Scott in 1864–65. The proximity of church and manor house gives the village an unusually strong historic character.
Penshurst Place:
A substantial, irregular manor house of sandstone, brick and ragstone, its picturesque silhouette enriched by battlements, towers and steep tiled roofs. The core is the great Baron’s Hall, built for Sir John de Pulteney in 1341, with an imposing chestnut roof and carved timber screen. A mid-C15 wing was followed by extensive Elizabethan additions, including a long gallery and the remodelled King’s Tower. Granted to the Sidney family by Edward VI in 1552, the house became their ancestral seat. C19 restoration by George Devey consolidated its Tudor character. The house stands amid formal walled gardens and a medieval deer park. It has been used for filming
Anne of the Thousand Days
(1969),
Elizabeth R
(1971),
The Princess Bride
(1987),
The Other Boleyn Girl
(2008),
Merlin
(2008),
Wolf Hall
(2015),
Mary Queen of Scots
(2018), and
Renegade Nell
(2024) among others.
The
route
(please click the link to see the route at the Ordnance Survey website):
Footpaths heading west from Chiddingstone Causeway, then southwest along a footpaths, will take us into Chiddingstone. Having admired the village, we will walk through the grounds of Chiddingstone Castle, crossing the lake and passing in front of the building. We will then head south along a lane to Hill Hoath, where we will join the Eden Valley Walk, a National Trail, before veering southeast towards another country lane. We will follow this in a southwesterly direction, before taking more footpaths to Smarts Hill, where we will stop for lunch at the pub. After lunch, we will walk around Smarts Hill and cross the B2188 to follow footpaths into Penshurst. We will then follow a footpath through Penshurst Park, affording good views of Penshurst Place. Emerging from the park at Cinder Hill, a short walk along a country lane, followed by a footpath, will take us to Moorden and then Station Hill, leading back to Penshurst Station.

Title: Channel Island Alderney Fort Clonque Experience
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a once-in-a-lifetime experience, as we fly off across the Channel to spend
four Nights on the magical island of Alderney
. Lying only a few miles off the Normandy shore, Alderney is part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey in the Channel Islands.
About Alderney
With history and human remains dating back to the last major ice-age, Alderney has been an island for the better part of ten thousand years. Measuring only four square miles, with one parish (St Anne's), it is the third largest of the Channel Islands and the only remaining continental possessions of a Crown brought to us by William the Conqueror. The major fortifications were started by Henry VIII as part of his defence of the realm and were continued throughout the next four hundred years.
The position of the Channel Islands so close to France made them a perfect place for privateers, many of whom grew rich on their spoils. Indeed much of this loot was spent on some of the fine buildings still extant on the island. New forts, expanded church and warehouses and quays.
During the Victorian period, the British Government funded the building and upgrading of thirteen forts and naval installations. Among these included a new, much enlarged breakwater and Fort Clonque.
During the second World War, the British War Office and Winston Churchill decided that they were unable to defend the Channel Islands. Alderney, with a population of c.1500 was entirely evacuated in June 1940 leaving a deserted island which the German forces occupied. They quickly set about building parts of the Atlantic Wall, four internment camps and dozens of buildings. Due to blockading by the Royal Navy and the war crimes committed on the island, islanders were unable to return home until December 1945. When they did they found their houses ransacked, burnt down or simply destroyed.
For several years the island operated as a communal farm, with all profits going into a Government backed fund aimed at rebuilding Alderney. By 1948 Alderney had established a measure of self governance and were moved from the Home Office to the Baliwick of Guernsey for legal, economic and governance functions. This included the running of the airport and harbour facilities.
With these changes the island was able to move from an almost exclusively arable economy to a more service and tourism based system. Being part of the Baliwick had significant tax and business benefits and several large multinational enterprises base themselves in Alderney.
Between beautifully soft, sandy beaches and impressive cliffs, Alderney and its surrounding islets support a rich flora and fauna. Trees are rather scarce, as many were cut down in the 17th century to fuel the lighthouses on Alderney and the Casquets. Those trees that remain include cabbage trees, due to the mild climate – often miscalled "palms" but of the lily family), and there are some small woods dotted about the island. Puffins on Burhou and gannets on Les Étacs (popularly called Gannet Rock) just off Alderney are a great draw for many visitors to the island.
The Accommodation
We will be staying in the beautifully restored
Fort Clonque - a
Landmark Trust property - which has rather comfortable space for thirteen of us to stay. Perched on a rocky outcrop, the Fort is linked to the rest of the island by a tidal causeway.
Warm, cosy wood lined rooms, open fires and breath taking views are on offer at our accommodation. Rooms are mostly twin rooms, with private bathrooms. Living quarters are spread across several small buildings around the central courtyard. Take a look at the location, for my meagre description could never do this amazing place justice! No Smoking  and there is Little to No Internet at Fort Clonque.
Getting to Fort Clonque from Alderney Airport.
There is only one way to Fort Clonque, and this will be walking on the road from the airport to the fort, following a zigzag path down a cliff to Fort Clonque. I believe the distance is just 1-2 miles from the Airport to Fort Clonque.
Outline Itinery
Monday 17th May 2027 - Arrive at Fort Clonque from 1700 onwards. Tea, coffee  and evening meal will be provided. Time to relax or see what the night life is like on Alderney, please be aware of the tide times, as Fort Clonque will get cut off by the tides.
Tuesday 18th May 2027 - After continental breakfast of cereals, toast, jam, marmalade and tea and coffee Provided, there will be a walk around the island. There may be places on the island where we can stop off for lunch (at extra cost). During or after the walk there may be a pub stop before going back to the fort. This evening, we will venture out and try some of the local cuisine (extra cost).
Wednesday 19th May 2027 -
After the continental breakfast we will venture out around the island, there maybe an option of a island trip by boat (extra cost). Sightseeing around the area. We will find somewhere to stop for lunch. Head back to the Fort in the afternoon where you can relax before our evening meal in.
Thursday 20th May 2027 - After continental breakfast we will decide as a group what to do as this is the last full day on the Island. We will stop off somewhere for lunch. Tonight we will eat out at a restaurant as its the last night on the island.
Friday 21st May 2027  - After continental breakfast we will need to clean the fort before we leave to head home. We will need to leave the fort by 10am. There may be a little time to spend on the island depending on everyone's flight times.

Title: Nottingham Bouldering (Lenton) - MONDAY - Beginners Welcome
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Nottingham’s newest bouldering venue
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?
As above, everyone attending the event  must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you are responsible for your own safety, actions and involvement at all times. As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive.) You can find the
link
to the waiver and bouldering safety video
here
on Nottingham Climbing Centre's website.
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
*Equipment hire charges will be waived for your first visit to the centre!
If you have any questions or need any more information just get in touch with the event leader by clicking on their profile below, or take a look at the
My first climbing event page
for more information.
IMPORTANT!
Please note that every person participating should be aware of (and accept) that those members perceived as ‘in charge’ or leading the event are not necessarily qualified, do not need to be qualified, and are not regarded by OutdoorLads, or themselves as ‘technical experts’ but are amateur climbers with some experience and who are happy to impart their knowledge. Any advice given should be considered with this in mind by the recipient.
All those attending the event must also be aware of the centre's own terms and conditions of participation and abide by them, along with any instructions given by the centre’s staff. Everyone must also take responsibility for their own safety while participating in Indoor climbing events.

Title: Autumnal Amble Around The Piethorne Valley
Summary:
The South Pennines area has the greatest density of reservoirs in the country. There are six lying in and around the Piethorne Valley. The reservoirs were constructed to meet the demands of the surrounding mill towns and canal systems, producing scenes of calm beauty amid the rugged upland of the Pennines.
Our 6 mile (10KM) walk in glorious rolling Pennine countryside passes five of them, as we take a route in varied landscapes of moorland, farmland and woodland. We will then finish the walk at a nice pub close by.
Part of our route follows the Greater Manchester Ringway

Title: Ambergate to Duffield - DVH Way Section 6
Summary:
The Derwent Valley Trust
was set up in 1996 to promote the history, arts, wildlife and leisure opportunities that surround the river Derwent along its 55 mile course through Derbyshire.
The Derwent Valley Heritage Way
takes us from Ladybower Reservoir in the Peak District National Park to its end at Derwent Mouth where it flows into the River Trent near Shardlow.
The route is divided into eight sections of between  ~13 km (8 miles) and ~17 km (10.5 miles), each with a clear public transport solution. All, except the first section, are linear routes. We park at the end, travel to the start, and walk back to our cars. Sections 5, 6, 7 are brilliantly served by the East Midlands Railway Derwent Valley Line
(Derby–Matlock, hourly), which runs almost parallel to the trail the whole way. For sections (2, 3, 4 and 8), we use local buses.
Each section is a walk in itself. Join one or more, as you wish, or walk all eight sections to complete the whole route through Derbyshire. Please ask other attendees for a lift if you need one.
Section 6 – Ambergate to Duffield ~14 km (8.7 miles) Total ascent 228 m (748 ft)
This part of the route takes us to woods and fields from Ambergate before passing a large pond as it heads for
Belper
, a town that retains much of its intriguing industrial past.
The town’s various mills loom into view as we approach Belper Bridge and the weirs. We pass the imposing East Mill and walk through the River Gardens before heading into the town centre.
Belper Park is a remnant of an old Royal forest. In the Middle Ages it was owned by the Duchy of Lancaster and used for breeding deer. From the park we head southwards to
Milford
where more factories were operated and powered by the Derwent.
At Makeney we will pause at the Holy Bush Inn for refreshments. From there we head across Duffield Bank, with fine views into the valley.
At Duffield Bridge we make a short detour to visit to
St Alkmunds Church
before heading to the station.
Well behaved
dogs are welcome
but must kept under control at all times.

Title: The Calf & Cautley Spout: A Hike through the Howgills
Summary:
Join Outdoor Lads for an early spring mountain walk in The Howgill Fells. Being lesser known than the neighbouring Lake District and Yorkshire Dales, these fells are often quieter with a remote feel.
This is a walk of two halves, with the first section, starting in Sedbergh,  being on lower ground, following the Pennine Journey trail along the River Rawthey. However, the walk suddenly gains elevation as we walk up Cautley Spout and on to the top of the fells. We'll then follow the Dales High Way trail over the summits of The Calf (676m) and Calders (674m) before dropping back down to Sedbergh.
Points of interest on the route:
The Pennine Journey Trail:
This long distance walking trail is a recreation of one of Wainwright's journeys. The section we'll follow takes us along the River Rawthey, giving us great views up to some of the Yorkshire Dales' Fells and also through some protected woodlands where red squirrels live.
Cautley Spout:
This spectacular waterfall is England's highest and becomes increasingly more impressive as we approach along Cautley Holme Beck, with the cliffs of Yarlside to the East and Cautley Craggs to the West. This is also the toughest part of the walk, with the trail up the side of the falls being particularly steep. Though this steepness will give us plenty of excuses to pause and admire the falls.
The Calf
: The final ascent to the summit of The Calf is nice and gentle after the slog up the waterfall. Once on the summit we'll be greeted with one of England's most expansive views; being able to see the Lake District's peaks to the North West and Morcombe Bay to the South West. To the North East we'll see the Pennines highest peaks, with the hills of the Yorkshire Dales to the South East. We'll head south from here, enjoying great views of the rest of The Howgill Fells
Other Information:
Dog Suitability:
Dogs are always welcome on my walks, though their behaviour and safety is their owner's responsibility. This includes cleaning up after them, controlling their behaviour around other animals or people, and assisting them over any stiles or streams we may cross.

to scan at the end of your run to record your finish time if you wish. However, you do not need to do this to take part in the run if you don't want to.
Course description:
The course is 5k long, run on tarmac, gravel and trail paths. It's three laps and starts and finishes at the circular tarmacked area near Akmal’s Tandoori Bistro, just up from the A660 Woodhouse Lane.
It is run on tarmac paths, with a small section of flagstones which can be uneven and slippery. There are sections of the course prone to potholes and uneven surfaces, so we ask that you take care and watch your footfall during the event.
From the start, head towards the roundabout directly ahead, going anti-clockwise around it and exiting along the sixth path (last exit before completing a full circle). At the end of this path, take a sharp right around the outside of the Queen Victoria statue (over the flagstones) and follow the tarmac paths clockwise around the park, with a nice downhill towards the Robert Peel statue. Be wary of some uneven sections. At the corner by the skate park & Robert Peel statue, take a sharp right uphill, then the first left. Continue straight ahead, over the start area, towards the Queen Victoria statue and your second lap. At the end of the third (final) lap, bear right up the hill towards the start area to reach the finish.
On occasion parkruns can be cancelled due to the weather or lack of volunteers. Should this happen I will try to contact members as soon as I can.

Title: Knaresborough Christmas Market - Circular walk from Bilton
Summary:
This is a circular 12.5K (8-mile) walk from the village of Bilton, through the Nidd Gorge and into Knaresborough. This is a relatively easy walk through beautiful broadleaf woodland. The route visits the Victorian Nidd Gorge Viaduct, 104 ft high, with seven arches and completed in 1848. It carried the North East Railway Line between Leeds and Thirsk and was closed in 1969. We will take some time to have lunch in Knaresborough and take in its
Christmas Markets
among a warren of medieval streets and stone staircases that weave their way up and down the hill. The town centre is perched on the cliffs above the River Nidd and the imposing railway viaduct. The walk returns through Conyngham Hall park, passing the Gardeners Arms pub, which you can stop at for a drink should you wish, though it will likely be getting dark by this point.
